utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Before we hear the witness, I see Mr. Morrissey standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: My apologies. Your Honours, good morning. I just wanted to raise a couple of matters now to pre-empt raising them later and entangling the witness in discussions about this. Your Honours, we don't have time today to deal with the matters that I have to raise but I have to put them on the record now because if I cross-examine upon a couple of things it might make it look as if we are accepting that they are part of the Prosecution case. Your Honours, as to the existence of an operations group and as to the relevance or existence of or otherwise of this Sandzak lobby that has now emerged, the Defence is concerned that these have got nothing no do with the indictment and nothing to do with the pleadings as they currently exist. Now, question arises as to how to deal with that now because there is really -- probably a matter of characterisation at the end of the case, but there is no evidence really at all, not really, there is no evidence at all of any -- of an operations group currently before the Court. Nor is there any evidence of any substance concerning the existence of a Sandzak lobby. Nevertheless, the Prosecution is -- has led evidence about them or attempted to do so from this witness. Now I'm in the position where I don't want to lend any validity to these ideas by cross-examining about them, but it's not appropriate to ask you the Tribunal to deliver an off-the-cuff ruling, an extemporary ruling on these matters and on the pleadings now. And it seemed to me what I wanted to do was to put on the record now that we don't accept that these have got anything to do with the indictment but that I will ask some questions about it now and thereby not waste the witness's time and still try to finish today. But when we come to argue the question of the operations group and the Sandzak lobby and what relevance these have, if any, to the case, I just want it on record now that I'm proceeding now on the basis that it's still going to be open to me later say it's irrelevant, even if I cross-examine on them. In other words the mere fact of cross-examining doesn't somehow build it into the pleadings. That's the reason I raise it now. I don't ask you to determine the matter or to make a ruling at all at this stage, and that can be dealt with later. If we have got a good argument, we'll win it; if we haven't we'll lose, frankly. I -- so I put those on the map anyway, at this stage, because I do propose to ask some questions about those topics, unless I've got clear coverage that then -- that they are irrelevant and not to be taken any notice of. Very well, that's the first thing. The next thing is that, Your Honour, because there is a number of important procedural things that have to be dealt with as well and they were supposed to be dealt with today or by today at all events, we might need to ask the Court to consider having a short Status Conference of some sort during the week next week. Now it's a matter for the Tribunal whether you have any time whatsoever or whether you have any interest in doing this, given the heavy schedule that you have. I understand that it's at short notice. But we have got a lot of outstanding correspondence with the Prosecutors we don't seem to be able to resolve this out of court, so there are some matters we are going to have to resolve in court. I won't say what the discussions have been; it doesn't matter what happens out of court. But we are going to have to ask to you help with some of those things. And there is also the two important issues I've already raised, the experts, so that's not one of them, but the future of the Karic deposition and what's to happen there. Whether the Prosecutor has any scheduling news to give us as to when they propose to have that deposition played, seeing that both sides agree it should be played, and the question is only in what form and when and how, that's the first one. And well, I note my learned friend, Ms. Chana, is not here and I won't raise things in her absence concerning the witness Delalic but there are a couple of issues we want to raise about Mr. Delalic as well, but I just put that on the map. Those are the reasons why we ask the Tribunal to consider whether it would be able to accommodate us for the purpose of some sort of Status Conference next, bearing in mind we are nearly at the end of the Prosecution case now and it will be too late to raise these things once we finish. When we come back from the break it appears there are four substantial witnesses left and then we're finished. So I raise those things now. I'm not asking Your Honours to do anything about it right now, I just think I have to put them on the record and maybe -- now, rather than complain later. So I do raise those things now and, perhaps later in the day, I could raise again the issue of whether we can be accommodated by the Tribunal or whether you have time or whether you will be prepared to do that to assist in -- during the time. I understand there is another proceeding going on, but the Defence would like that if it could be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, could I ask you a question? I believe that you indicated that you will be not available next week. So could you please tell me whether we will be back and what's the proper time for us to have that Status Conference?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Tribunal doesn't have to dance at my convenience. I'm grateful for the inquiry. I shall be back in The Hague on Tuesday, late on Tuesday, so Wednesday, Thursday, or Friday would all be acceptable from the Defence. Wednesday and Thursday would be acceptable, I think, from the Defence point of view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. At this moment, not everything is in our hands because we have six cases going on simultaneously and some courtroom needs to be maintained. So I have to consult with the Registrar to see if logically it's possible or not for the Status Conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I just indicate this? In terms of the matters that would be raised at the Status Conference, my learned friend Mr. Mettraux would be well and truly able to represent the Defence at that, so that if an opportunity arose on a day when I was not around, that would be acceptable from the Defence point of view and the Prosecution also may have its timing issues to be taken into account so if you can accommodate us then, any time will suit and if I can't be there, Mr. Mettraux will be able to handle those matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. As for the other two issues, popped up in the direct examination, one's the operation group, the other is the Sandzak group, and my preliminary response is that I did not see any relevance for that Sandzak group. Because it's not appeared in the indictment, I fail to see the relevance to our case, I mean direct relevance, at this stage. Maybe later on there will be some lights shed by the parties on that issue. As for the operational group, I believe that, as I said yesterday, the operational group is not a kind of special force -- I mean the operational group was not capitalised. It's just a way to describe the inspection team, to my understanding. Of course, you have the full right to cross-examine on that issue, but this is my understanding at this stage. Maybe Mr. Re could shed more light on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's quite correct, Your Honour. It is -- an operational group under JNA doctrine was a group formed for a specific tags being such as the 2nd operational group in the Strugar case, which was used to blockade Dubrovnik. It's formed for a specific task. It could be combat, it can be a specific other purpose, and some evidence is available that the inspection team had the same function as an operational group. So in one respect it really is only a matter of terminology, but it also goes to the issue of command and control. On the issue of the Sandzak lobby it only goes this far: There may be evidence that there was something called a Sandzak lobby and Celo from Sandzak and Mr. Halilovic being from Sandzak, that is -- could be the reason why he chose Celo to go to -- on our case, to go to Grabovica. So, it's not a -- it's not a -- it's not a huge part of the Prosecution case but there could be some evidence on it. It's not a matter of pleading. It's an evidentiary matter. It's not a material fact. But it could form part of the -- the whole tapestry. There is just -- the others things my learned colleague, Mr. Morrissey, pointed to, the Karic depositions, it's not correct that the Prosecution agree that they should be played. The Prosecution said quite clearly we -- we resist them being played and Court time being used for them being played. We are of course in the Trial Chamber's hands. The Trial Chamber should of course view them, but we say preferably not in invaluable court time. But it's a matter for the Trial Chamber. The other thing was the necessity for a Status Conference. The -- the Prosecution doesn't see at the moment -- of course we are in the Trial Chamber's hands, the necessity for a Status Conference to discuss any of the matters my learned colleague raised, when we come back, he says this is for four witnesses. We anticipate there will be at least two weeks of -- of evidence in that, probably with some days spare, in which any of the outstanding evidentiary issues can be resolved. And finally on the matter of outstanding correspondence, I'll give an undertaking here, we'll have -- we'll have any outstanding correspondence resolved by mid next week, which is when the Status Conference would probably occur. So, if that doesn't happen, my learned friends are of course entitled to come back and lay complaint to the Trial Chamber about our tardiness in that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could I ask you who will be the next witness after we resume the proceedings? Is that the pathologist planned?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, it will be as planned, it will be the pathologist, whose name I can't quite recall, "Andalejovic" or something like -- followed by Ramiz Delalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Well, for the information of the parties, I believe that we made decisions yesterday concerning the provisional release filed by the Defence. As for the Karic decisions, it will be delivered today or next Monday. It depends on how we proceed, because as you understand that, we have a very, very busy week, and yesterday I have five sittings in this courtroom. So it's hard to find any time to go into the details of anything. But anyway, we will consider the requests from the Defence for a Status Conference sometime next week. At the same time, we will bear in mind the objections from the Prosecution. Well, could we have the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is being brought in, just on the last matter you raise the which was the provisional release decision, the -- we note that the application was filed confidentially. The Prosecution's view of this is it's not a matter which should be dealt with confidentially, an application for provisional release mid-trial. If there are matters that -- medical matters or private matters which shouldn't be in the public domain, they should really be in a confidential schedule, because a matter of provisional release mid-trial is a matter of public interest as, of course, would be -- in our submission the -- the Trial Chamber's decision. We would ask if there is a decision that has to be filed, that, if it could be made, we would request that it be made public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I do remember about confidentiality of these filings but we discuss it in the open court the other day.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we did. We agree with the Prosecution to the extent that as far as possible all filings should be done in a non-confidential basis. The only reason why this was done in this case was that within the filing itself there were references to threats being made to a person which Your Honour will remember, and we thought better and safer to make reference to those matters in confidential -- in a confidential fashion. For the rest we agree with our colleagues that in general those applications should be made on a non-confidential basis. But that was the reason why it was done, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. We will look into the -- all the filings in this matter and see whether there is a necessity to lift the confidentiality on that. Of course, we will take your submissions into consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, good morning, witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe today is the last day for your stay in The Hague. We will try our best to send you home today. Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Karavelic. Yesterday, before we finished, you gave evidence concerning some attempts to bring the 9th Brigade and the 10th brigade into the line of command and control and now I want to move to another step. Having considered the steps taken by Hajrulahovic and Sefer Halilovic early in June and having considered the report given by the commission involving Maslak and Bilajac, I now want to turn to another body. Do you recall an institution called the Council for the Protection of the Constitutional Order?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I seem to vaguely recall something like that but I can't really say much about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. This was not a purely military body, was it, the Council for the Protection of the Constitutional Order?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And that was a body that was attended, I understand that you weren't -- were not normally present at it, but to your knowledge that was a body that involved the highest levels of government and in particular ministers from that government. Is that -- was that your understanding at the time?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's so but I really can not be certain about all the particulars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, I understand that. The questions I have for you about that are, I have to say, very general ones. But did you on one occasion provide information to that council, broadly in the terms that you've provided to this Tribunal, namely that the 9th and the 10th Brigades were not in the line of command and control?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I'm not sure, but I'm not ruling out the possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand. Just -- I take it you were pretty busy at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: We have heard evidence from other witnesses concerning that particular council. Can you just tell us, in the normal course of events, if that council wanted to hear from a military person such as yourself, in what form would they seek that information? Would they ask you to go there and speak to them or would they seek a report from you in written form?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that most often it would be the second case, that you would send a written report and then subsequent steps would be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, in terms of your own contribution, I appreciate you can't remember any -- any particular contacts that you had, but from the time you were appointed as 1st Corps commander in August, you made it quite clear, both to Rasim Delic, your commander, and also to the president of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, that you wanted a political decision made to allow you to deal with command and control issues in the 1st Corps; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And really, at that time, you understood that if you were to deal with the -- the 9th and 10th Brigades' command and control problems in a military way, that would require very significant resources and very significant planning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And it's the fact that you were not able to deal with those units without support at the highest political level, namely the level of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just to establish this point a little bit further, when you did finally come to deal with that problem, you had to mount a massive operation involving something in the order of 5.000 combat troops and police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And I just want to ask you about some of the other preparations that were -- that had to be done at a military level by you and your subordinates. There had to be -- the troops who you were going to use in that operation to bring the 9th and 10th into the line of command and control had to be given some morale type of preparation and some morale support for the job they were going to do; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You also had to be sure that counterintelligence manoeuvres were in place to stop the Serbs from finding out -- the Republika Srpska army from finding out that there might be trouble in the town; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And there was another problem that you faced and that was the danger that other units might seek to intervene, might potentially, possibly seek to intervene to help the 9th and 10th Brigades if you didn't take proper steps to protect against that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I Just briefly want to ask you a question about the 2nd Independent Battalion in that regard. The 2nd Independent Battalion, to your knowledge, were a very patriotic, multi-ethnic unit who were very good fighters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And you were very hopeful that they wouldn't get themselves caught up in the trouble of Operation Trebevic when the 9th and 10th had to be dealt with; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's why I had to take particular steps in relation to that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And one of the concerns -- you tell -- I want to put a proposition. You tell me if this is accurate, and you might be able to make a comment on it. One of the concerns that the 2nd Independent Battalion appeared to have was that any cleanup of the 9th and 10th Brigade might be a move in favour of the police and against the army. Was that a concern that the 2nd Independent Battalion leadership expressed to you at various times or at any time?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not so directly, but it's possible that it was done implicitly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It -- it was a constant problem that you had to deal with that the soldiers on the line were suspicious of the police authorities and in Trebevic, too, you knew you had to use police authorities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And so as a result of that, you invested considerable time to persuade the 2nd Independent Battalion that they had nothing to fear from this operation and that they should not become involved in a civil strife in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And apart from the 2nd Independent Battalion there was other units that you took precautionary measures against to block certain roads and so on, just in case they decided to intervene in the Operation Trebevic; is that correct too?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, I appreciate I've jumped forward to the Trebevic operation in taking you to those details, but back in August of 1993, when you first raised this matter, the political will to undertake such a major task appeared to you to be lacking; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I think, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And in the end, you had to bring significant pressure to bear, including a threat of resignation, before you were able to secure that written authority that you wanted to take military steps to bring the 9th and 10th back into control; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And one of the documents that you needed to have produced was a document from the Presidency, from Alija Izetbegovic, terminating the commission of Musan Topalovic as the brigade commander of the 10th Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And some others as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And -- was also -- just to be clear, was one of those others Ramiz Delalic?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just as an extra question on that, Fikret Prevljak, once again, managed to retain his position at the 4th Hrasnica Brigade, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right. I understand that. Are you able now to remember when it was that you got the -- the -- the document from Alija Izetbegovic indicating that he hereby removes from their positions of command Ramiz Delalic, Musan Topalovic and other individuals? Do you recall when you saw that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was just before the action at Trebevic. I don't know whether a day or two before, or on the very day. I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Thanks very much. So moving back to August, I asked you the question about the political will to get rid or to deal with these units, and you've given the answer about that. At that time, you had a real concern about the 9th and 10th Brigades, I suggest to you, and you comment on this. It wasn't just that they were out of the line of command and control themselves, but you saw a real danger that if they stayed out of the line of command and control, that sort of behaviour would have a very negative effect on neighbouring units that were holding crucial parts of the front line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And in particular, you were concerned about the effect that these -- that the 9th and 10th and their behaviour -- perhaps I should make this clear, the leadership of the 9th and the 10th and their behaviour would have on the 1st and 2nd Brigades which held the adjoining parts of the front line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And just to put this -- we have been dealing in a sense at a level of abstraction but, in practical terms, did it pose problems for you as a commander in trying to maintain command and control of the other units that these other units would say, "How come we have to obey the rules and you don't do anything about the 9th and the 10th brigades whether they break the rules?" Did you have to deal with that sort of problem and that sort of inquiry from other soldiers?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had an enormous number of problems in that respect. There were even requests from some, so to say, good brigade commanders who tended to say even if you don't give your approval we are going to go ahead and attack them. For example, I had one example, and in that case it would have been actually a disaster had it happened in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Is one example of that sort of behaviour the incident you described where Senad Hasic, the loyal friend of or loyal subordinate of Musan Topalovic had that cannon trained in your direction?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's just one example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And if the Tribunal needs to know about this, I'm not going to ask you for the details about this now, but if the Tribunal needs to know about other examples you've got plenty of other examples you could tell, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And I suppose in short, to -- this is just to capture your position, whether as a deputy under the command of Mustafa Hajrulahovic, Talijan, and also under the command of Sefer Halilovic, when he was in charge of the army, or as corps commander, yourself, under the command of Commander Delic, you yourself wanted action to be taken to bring these units in, and you yourself supported any action taken by your superiors to attempt to bring those units under the line of command and control. Was that your position?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the next series of questions concern the realities of how to deal with the 9th and 10th Brigade in the real situation that you found yourself in. As a general proposition, you as commander simply had to live with and to work with Ramiz Delalic and, to the extent possible, Musan Topalovic, because they were defending your front line in the 1st Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And in the situation that you were in, when you wanted them to do something, you had to rely on persuasion to get them to cooperate; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: For example, when Ramiz Delalic was on one side of the street with his guns and soldiers and Boris Krstanovic was on the other side and you went out and intervened and stopped a blood bath from happening, you used persuasion and an appeal to their better nature to stop the disaster from happening; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And when Caco -- I'm sorry, when Musan Topalovic had that -- had the showdown with Mujo Zulic of the 1st Brigade that you described, again you had to use persuasion to stop a disaster from happening; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: In a normal army, where the system of command and control was maturely developed and in place, the way to deal with those sort of incidents is that you would send in the military police, arrest the wrongdoers and have them dealt with by the relevant legal process; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That wasn't an option available to you because the system of command and control in the Bosnian army at that time was immature and because Ramiz Delalic and his units, and Musan Topalovic and his units, were not integrated into the system of command and control; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Incidentally, I just mentioned the name Mujo Zulic before and I just wanted to ask you a question about him. We've spoken in this Court about a number of rumours, pieces of gossip and bits of information concerning other people. There was plenty of rumours, gossip and nonsense being talked about Mujo Zulic as well, wasn't there, at that time, if you wanted to listen to rumours, gossip and nonsense?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not quite understood the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm really asking, because it's been said that there was rumours about Ramiz Delalic and rumours about Caco, and Musan Topalovic, so I'm just asking you whether there was rumours about other people too, and including -- and I'm using Mujo Zulic as an example. Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there were quite a few rumours about Mujo Zulic as well. If you need some more information about him, I can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, really what I'm concerned to establish here is just the simple point. You can tell us if it's right. There was a lot of rumours about a lot of people in Sarajevo at that time, it wasn't limited to Ramiz Delalic and Musan Topalovic among the commanders; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. The entire time, amongst other things, I had also been referring to that in the course of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that. All right. Thank you. Now, however, there was a war to fight and Sarajevo had to be defended against daily attacks from the Army of the Republika Srpska, and so you continued to try to work with these units even though they were outside the line of control and command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even if they were not in the line of command and control 100 per cent, and, yes, and the second part of the question, yes, I do agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And turning now to the brigade of Ramiz Delalic briefly, to your knowledge, in that brigade, there were a number of Croatian persons, including the chief of security, Tomo Juric; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, both the 9th and the 10th Brigade were units from which it was and had already proved over time from which it was possible to detach small numbers of soldiers at short notice to be used in emergency situations elsewhere. Now I'm going to give you some examples but, in general, is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not just from those units and those brigades. It was possible from other brigades as well, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm just going to show you an example of an order dealing with those particular troops, and others, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown -- sorry, just excuse me a moment, please. Pardon me, I just have to bring this up on the -- thanks. Your Honours, this is Defence document 65 ter number 216 and it's DD001099. There is a paper copy for the Prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI 400.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I just indicate that as to the provision of paper copies, we are going to provide -- attempt to provide an a paper copy of each document we show to the witness to the Prosecution. It's a matter -- one of the matters we want to raise at the Status Conference later on because it's -- we are using the E-court and we have to use the E-court, but because the Prosecutor has indicated in his motion some difficulties in using the screen simultaneously we are prepared to provide those paper copies here today. But we don't want to say -- we don't want to pre-empt the ruling that Your Honour might give on this topic, on this motion later on. So in saying what I'm saying I just want to protect our position in terms of that motion, but -- so as not to delay things with argument now, we are going to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At this stage, maybe you could remind me whether you filed something in response to the Prosecution's motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I thought we had, Your Honour. I thought we had some days ago, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. I think I have to check it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, we -- certainly one was produced because I looked at it. If it hasn't -- if it's miscarried we will give you a copy of it straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It has been filed. We do have a copy of it. It opposes the motion, but I'd like to express my gratitude for -- our gratitude for my learned friend providing us with paper copies, at least with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thanks, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Karavelic, it's an E-court dispute that you don't have to be worried by. Now, just -- do you have that order in front of you now, that order of the 18th of the August?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And among other obviously the units from the 9th and 10th are not the only units that you detached, but it is the fact that you ordered the detachment of some of their troops to go out on Igman to assist in operations -- defensive operations out there; is that correct? First I should ask you, is that an order that you issued? I should get the formalities straight first. Is that an order issued by you on the 18th of August moving certain units out to Igman to assist the position out there?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's my name and my signature, and I had referred to this order in the course of my testimony before. I had mentioned it --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- is what I meant to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You did -- you mentioned an order dated the 18th of August, and I just wanted to know if this was the order you were talking about.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Thanks. Your Honours, I offer that document for tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There is no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. It's admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D400.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether you can remember this but please tell us if you can remember. On that particular occasion, can you remember whether you spoke to Mr. Imsirevic or Mr. Delalic prior to issuing that order concerning the 9th Brigade? If you can remember, tell us; if not, well, we understand that too.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember. More likely I did not. Perhaps I did. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I won't pursue it in that event. Very well. Could the witness now be shown another document please, this one is Defence 65 ter number D218. Sorry, it's admitted we think as D257. Yes, it's Exhibit D257. This is a later order - I'm showing it to you as an example of such orders - concerning the movement of one unit from the 10th Brigade on the 6th of September. It may or may not have any connection at all to the units that you sense down to Herzegovina and I'm going to ask you that question. Do you have that document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Morrissey this document has yet to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm The Court deputy just indicated -- yet to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document MNA is not admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, it's not admitted. Very well. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay, well, anyway, in regard to this particular document here, is this an order of yours returning a part of the 10th Brigade back to its -- back to Sarajevo at least, because of favourable military developments on Igman?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And do you recall now -- you may or may not recall -- do you recall now whether any soldiers from that unit were taken down to Herzegovina when those troops -- when the 10th Brigade troops that went to Herzegovina actually left or not?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I can't really confirm anything there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: In fact, just to clinch that closed, do you have any memory of the particular reasons why that unit was brought back to -- to Sarajevo at that time or not?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean, what it says in the document, and although what I know, is that in the course of the war, considering the situation and considering the reasons for writing a document or an order, you would always refer to the actual reasons in the said document. So there is nothing but the truth with regard to the actual situation, which is the reason why I'm withdrawing this unit, but perhaps prior to that, I don't know whether there had been any problems or any complaints about individual soldiers of that 10th Mountain Brigade -- at Igman. I don't know, but had it happened, presumably it would have been in this order. I never intended to write orders in one way, trying to imply something else, and something else is the real reason why I'm doing it. I never used that before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: To be clear we are not suggesting to you that you did. And in addition to what you've just said there, it's the fact that you would never in an order have concealed anything wrong done by the 10th Brigade because it was your desire to bring them into line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. And there are quite a few documents referring to all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. But let me just put this question to you as a general proposition. When you used -- when you yourself used units from the 9th Brigade, units from the 10th Brigade, outside of Sarajevo, you did not expect them to slaughter innocent civilians of any nationality whatsoever; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least, and without wanting to insult anyone at all, but I think it's not serious and it's ridiculous, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You're not insulting any one. Sometimes we have to ask very basic questions here and I'm grateful for your patience in answering them. As far as you knew, as you've indicated, most of the soldiers, most of the individual soldiers from these units were just good boys, patriotic, and not criminals; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Of course, you knew that the leadership had involved itself in some trench-digging activities, you'd heard rumours about rackets, and you knew about problems with the line of control and command. But what I suggest to you is this: There was nothing that suggested that a nightmare set of killings like those at Grabovica would occur; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that -- and I do apologise. In my previous answer to your previous question, when you said, if I may repeat what you said, that most of them were not criminals, I would like to reformulate that. I mean, I agreed with you, but it would follow that some of them were indeed criminals, but not a single member of these units was ever described as a criminal in any way. This is a fact. I mean, not just the majority. I kind of glossed over it, but I just like to put it right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And I just want to jump forward to the individual selection of the troops that went down to Herzegovina. The fact is that you yourself absolutely did not hand pick the individuals who took the journey down to Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And furthermore --

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise. That wasn't my job either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That was my next question. As corps commander, it just wasn't your role to select those individuals. That was a job for someone much lower down the hierarchy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And in fact, although you might have met one or two of the soldiers for one reason or another in the course of your duties, it wasn't necessary for you to know those individuals personally at all; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. I did not know them. Perhaps two, three, five people, tops; soldiers, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: At the time when they were lined up -- I shouldn't say "they" because they are separate units. I'll deal with the 9th Brigade troops that went down there first of all. To the extent that you can remember them lining up at the Trampina street barracks and then setting off on their journey, and so far as you can remember that, did it appear to you that the people who went down there to Herzegovina in that unit were in fact volunteers?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that it was so to a large extent but it does not have to be true totally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just to be clear about that, do you have a very clear memory about that lineup or is it a bit long ago?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I do remember that lineup. It was brief, it was not at the barracks, it was in the street. Close to Titova street, next to the command of the 9th Motorised Brigade. I think -- I don't know whether it was that morning that day or the day before. I think it was that morning on the day that the unit was supposed to set off, and in the course of those preparations, as to whether I came on purpose in order to address the units and to take a look at the unit, because they were the closest to the command of the corps. The command of the 9th Motorised Brigade was the closest alongside the reconnaissance and sabotage brigades. Those two commands were closest to the corps command at 50- and 150-metre distance respectively. So I addressed them for five, six minutes, very briefly. And nothing -- there was absolutely nothing to indicate that anything bad or anything out of the ordinary was likely to happen. Everything was absolutely ordinary, as I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And when -- when you spoke to these troops, I understand you may not recall the exact words that you used to them, but I suppose you said in words that they -- well, I ask you this: In general terms, did you say in words that they could understand, "Boys, fight well, don't hurt the civilians, and behave properly while you're down there"?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that every single word that you've just uttered must certainly be a part of that five-minute address on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Because that's the sort of thing you always said when you were talking to troops, to give them some motivation?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You didn't have a written-out text of that speech, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. I never had that in writing. I mean, it was always off the cuff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand that. Now -- very well. Now, I jumped forward. Perhaps I should ask you this question: Do you recall whether or not you spoke to the units from the 10th Brigade which went down there before they left?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no. I don't think so. Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I offer the order that's on the screen here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There is no objection, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But I have some doubts about this document. What's the relevance of our case here? I fail to see the direct relevance to the troops moved to Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It's just to show that these troops could be moved around without fear. Even though they were out of the line of command and control, that in terms of detaching them from one place and taking them to another, when I come -- when I come to the discussions that took place, I'm going to be putting that it was perfectly sensible to choose to take these units down to Herzegovina, and I want to establish why that is by pointing out that they been used in the past, in military operations, that they had been detached sensibly in the past. So it's part of the Prosecution's case I take it, Your Honours, well, I'll go on if you need me to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, in this sense and since there is no objections from the Prosecution, this document is admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours I'd have to concede it's on the B list. Now, could I just ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I was informed that this document was earlier marked as under seal document. Are there any particular reasons for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It may have been put a witness at a particular time. There is nothing about the document itself, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. So you don't ask for the confidential?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Can I just consult to make sure I'm not making a mistake?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours we don't think there is any problem about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Court deputy will announce the number of that document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D257.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, before we come to the events in Herzegovina, I understand we've jumped forward into those events a couple of times, but I just want to ask you about two more things that happened in the months of July and August, which may have relevance to this case. The first of those is what happened to -- what happened to Sefer Halilovic and there are just a couple of documents I want to show you about that. Just excuse me. Sorry, Mr. Karavelic. I've got into trouble with my papers here. I think I can proceed without the papers. I'll just ask you the questions. You've indicated -- I've asked you questions in the past about -- about Mr. Halilovic being -- I've asked you some questions in the past about Mr. Halilovic being replaced by Rasim Delic as the number one man in the army and I won't repeat those, but I want to come now to an order that was passed on the 18th of July -- there is an order of the 18th of July which clarified the structure of the senior leadership of the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, I'm sorry could I just indicate why there is fluffing at the bar table? This was all on a sheet of paper and the relevant documents to go to which has now vanished. I know the questions to ask and just as soon as we can identify, or re-identify that document, I can proceed. So, if I could just ask -- I apologise to those helping me for that slip. Just excuse me while we find that, please, Mr. Karavelic. Yes, could the witness please be shown Exhibit 143? And in particular page 5 of that exhibit. Perhaps show the first page and then -- then once the witness has had a chance to look at that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have on the screen in front of you now a document headed decision on the organisational structure of the Ministry of Defence and the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours in this situation, what I might do is ask that the witness be provided with a paper copy of this document because it's lengthy and has annexes to it. What I'm doing is providing the Bosnian copy to the witness. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: This is-- this a lengthy document. You have the full right to read it if you feel the need to, but I might try to ask you a couple of questions before you read the whole thing because I'm only going to take you to a very narrow part of it. First of all, are you familiar with this document under the hand of the president of the Bosnian presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, and dated the 18th of July 1993?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, in that event, could I ask you to look at the fifth page which is a diagram or a chart of the organisation -- organisational chart of the Main Staff of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's on page 5 of the English. It's a chart. And could I just ask that the Court staff assist to the best extent that they can in having the document rotated in the relevant way so that it can be read?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well, thanks. I just want to get some explanations from you here about the line of -- at a very basic level for those of us who are not military people, as to what this document says about certain aspects of the line of command and control. Now, that document reveals that the commander of the -- has a position of the commander of the General Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. At the time, that commander was Rasim Delic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, under commander Delic, there are three deputy commanders, two of whom are just simply deputy commanders, and one of whom is a deputy commander by virtue of being the Chief of the Main Staff. That person at this time being Sefer Halilovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The other two deputy commanders were Jovo Divjak and Stjepan Siber, a Serbian person and Croatian person by ethnicity, respectively?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And that arrangement of army matters answered to a higher political requirement that the -- that is revealed in the platform that you've showed us at the start of your evidence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, in the line of command, the 1st Corps of which you were the -- the head, perhaps just so that -- so that the transcript clearly reflects realities here, the 1st Corps commander was you, Mr. Karavelic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Who was the 2nd corps commander?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, Sead Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Who was the 3rd Corps commander?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: August 1993, it was Enver Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The 4th Corps was Arif Pasalic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arif Pasalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now the 5th Corps was somewhat isolated far to the north in Bihac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Who was the commander of that corps?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think at the time it was still Ramiz Drekovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Commander of the 6th Corps was Salko Gusic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And the 7th Corps and the 8th Corps had yet to come into being in any real sense; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the time they didn't exist yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, the line of reporting of command and control from the corps level at which you were to the next level up, there was a line directly between Commander Delic and the corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Do you see in the bottom right-hand corner a section entitled "legend," and it describes the function of the solid line and of the dotted line, do you see that section?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The English translator was unable to work out what those words were. What's the word next to the solid line and what's the word next to the dotted line?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very small. I assume it says "commanding," and the second word could be "saradnja," "cooperation." That could be next to the dotted line. I assume that's it. It's very small. I can't read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You assume that because, although on this particular chart it may be difficult to read, nevertheless, given your knowledge of the situation at the time, that is in fact what those lines must mean; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now I have to ask you some questions about the powers of the Chief of Staff, and to come to the crunch, in this -- matters that are relevant to this case, the Chief of Staff was a person who could issue a combat order if the commander authorised him to do so; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Simply by virtue of his office as Chief of Staff, he did not have the right, without such an authorisation to issue commands to you as the commander of a corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: But of course, if he was supported, if he was authorised by the Supreme Commander, in this case Rasim Delic, then he could do whatever he was authorised to do by that Supreme Commander, is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And therefore at a general level of abstraction like this, the question whether or not a Chief of Staff has got power to command combat operations or combat activities is always to be resolved by reference to one thing, and that is: What power did the commander give him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I -- the function of the Chief of Staff at any level of any unit or at the level of the staff as a whole, is one of the key posts as far as planning, monitoring, and control is concerned. And then when I say "control," it's hard to translate. It means that they have constant oversight of the combat operations, and anything that has to do with combat operations, that would be the staff to prepare any kind of decisions, guidelines, directives, in terms of what to do at that point in time, tomorrow, in the future, how to conduct the conduct -- the combat operations. This is prepared by the staff of that command, together with the Chief of Staff, and it's prepared for the commander of that unit or the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This would be it, roughly, generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And in the course of combat operations, does a Chief of Staff, even though not having any direct power to issue commands, have the competence and the right to explain and clarify to the subordinate junior units what is the meaning of the order of the commander to whom that Chief of Staff is attached?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he does have that right, and it's a kind of obligation and duty for him, because the orders which are issued by the main commander, for example, are something that the Chief of Staff would understand the best, because it was the Chief of Staff who prepared that for the commander and not the commander who did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And when the Chief of Staff issues -- when the Chief of Staff issues an explanation, let's say during a combat operation the Chief of Staff is -- finds himself in a position where he needs to explain the commander's order to someone down the line, how does he do that? Does he issue an order to the people down the line or does he issue an instruction to those people down the line, or an advice? What's the mechanism by which he should do that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of those options are possible. It depends on the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: In the situation where a Chief of Staff issues an order to one of the units down the line, is he entitled to do that in order to clarify and give expression to the original order of the commander?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're talking about an order as well as providing an explanation. This is a little bit counter to one another. In the military jargon, if it's an order, it's an order; if it's an explanation, then it's an explanation. However, I'm not ruling out the possibility of something like that happening, but it's not customary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And I should ask you this, in terms of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I ask, please, that the -- I'm just being distracted a little bit -- I'm sorry I didn't raise this, but it's been going on for 20 minutes. I'm being distracted by talking and I ask that it stop now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, just to press on about that, in terms of the rights of the Chief of Staff at the -- at the level of this chart here, the Chief of Staff has got a command power over certain of his branches that are under his direct power, according to that chart; is that correct? In other words, can the Chief of the Main Staff command his staff within the staff?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And he had the full command only over the staff within his headquarters, and this is the part that is marked in black, the squares that are in this part that is highlighted in black, but it's not clear to me why the operations centre is not also in that black square. It's maybe clear why they did it on this particular diagram but according to what I think it should be within this highlighted area, it's probably not included in the staff, in terms of full command, probably because the operation centre also includes officers and staff from these other parts of the Main Staff Command. However, I think that the operation centre should also be under the control of the Chief of Staff. This is just a little point or a note when we are talking about the organisational scheme.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm grateful to you for raising it because I was going to ask you that question. According to that chart, does it appear that the Chief of Staff here has been given the power over the operations centre?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And what other -- well, perhaps -- the question I'm really coming to is this: When you're considering the usual powers of a Chief of Staff, does the Chief of Staff normally have under his competence the administration for organisation and mobilisation affairs and also the intelligence administration? Now I understand he doesn't on this scheme but usually speaking, in military organisation, does the Chief of Staff normally have those under his power?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to clarify something. I don't know the exact dates when certain changes were made. For a time, the intelligence and the security sections, especially the intelligence section, were in the staff. Then they were taken out of the staff and then returned again. But I think that, generally, the intelligence section remained part of the staff under the command of the Chief of Staff, but the security section was never under the command of the Chief of Staff. This first part that you mentioned, I don't know. What did you say before the intelligence, if you can say that again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I can probably clarify it by pointing to the chart. If you look at the left-hand side of the chart you'll see that there is a series of branches that are set out in boxes there, and the two I was asking you about was Roman numeral V, administration for administration and mobilisation affairs, and Roman numeral II, intelligence administration. And my question really is this: You'll see that the black line indicating the line of command goes from those two branches back to the commander, but only a dotted line appears to go from those back to the Chief of Staff. And what I wanted to know is does this appear to you to be -- to be somewhat of a reduction of the usual powers of a Chief of Staff, according to this diagram?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. If we look at the left side of the administrations, you have the administration of the services, of the air force, the administration for organisational and mobilisation affairs, intelligence administration, section for the navy and also the administration for -- I can't read it and I can't remember what it is. These administrations are directly under the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The staff with each of these administrations had the line of cooperation between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that. Now, the next issue I want to move to is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, just out of curiosity, Mr. Morrissey, could I ask you a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you have a similar chart outlining the military structure in the 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: What we would do -- because the witness has given evidence about this we can simply provide photocopies of that document because it was a contemporaneous document. If Your Honour would like us to draft one that's -- sorry, pardon me. 1st Corps? I misunderstood the question, my apologies. Perhaps I could pursue that with the witness for a moment and see. I don't have one but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I understand, since we have this witness here, he's the commander of the 1st Corps, and it might be good for us to get some information about the military structure under the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well with respect I agree entirely. I can ask some questions about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I actually have one the witness drew. It's a handwritten one. He drew it outside of court. We didn't get it typed up. That may be of some assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe during the break the parties could meet together to see whether it's useful or not. Do you agree with that, Mr. Morrissey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm happy to. I'll just ask a couple of questions about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: In fact, did the Prosecutors ask you to draw up a similar sort of diagram concerning the structure of the 1st Corps before we came into court last week? And did you in fact draw one up?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of last week, I just did it by hand on a piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, perhaps it would assist the Court if you were able to draft a document that is as similar in form as possible to the one that you've just been looking at so it could be compared to, if needs be, in the future. If that's already been done, fine, if you'd like to do another one, that's also fine. Would you be prepared to draw such a document in the break that we are about to have now?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can do that, but I cannot be sure about exactly the time period that you are looking for. If you give me a time period, then I cannot be sure whether the situation was the way it was during that particular period, because the transformations were on going from throughout that whole period. I told the Prosecution regarding the organisation that it was like that, but I'm not 100 per cent sure. If we are talking about the intelligence organ I think that later, and I can't tell you exactly when, that the intelligence organ only was returned or -- to be a part of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, perhaps if you -- if you were able to draft it to the best of your memory now and then when -- when you're -- if you're asked questions about it, you can indicate what areas you were 100 per cent sure about and which once ones you possibly had some doubts about. Just before we break, there was one other diagram I was going to ask you -- ask you to -- to draw, and that was a rough diagram of Sarajevo and where the units were placed around Sarajevo. In other words, I understand you haven't have a topographical map but just a schematic map with 1st Corps, 10th -- 1st Brigade, 10th Brigade, and the way it was around Sarajevo just to give us a function ago idea where these units were in relation to each other. And in doing so it might assist if you marked down where those units were and also where a couple of crucial headquarters were, headquarters of the 9th, headquarters of your corps, headquarters of the Chief of Staff, headquarters of the army, and if you wouldn't mind drawing that in just rough form that would assist, or could assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I indicate that the -- that the next topic is going to be the Zenica conference? And before we break, perhaps I can just indicate what's proposed to be done. The Zenica conference is -- is a tape. I'm going to ask the witness to look at a tape and just verify that -- that that's him, and indeed all of the people there, he can name the people that he can recognise there, and listen to a short part of what he says himself, also a short part of what Mr. Halilovic said at that Zenica meeting. And then I'm going to seek to tender that tape. Now the whole tape, not everything said on that tape it is relevant to this case and the reason the Defence wants to tender is because of what's not said on that tape. Because there is -- what we will say is there is no reference to some of the things that are said in the indictment. The indictment says certain things about Zenica and we have this tape. There is a tape and there is a transcript of the tape. I don't propose to play the whole thing to the witness. I just propose to tender it. I understand the Prosecution must have -- have some version of this because there is already evidence that the witness Salko Gusic was shown that document on a previous occasion. Nevertheless it's important that it be in evidence in case anyone was to say anything about what was said at Zenica. I'm going to ask this witness from his memory, of course, but that's what's proposed, so we will cue up the tape to the parts we want. But I make it clear I'm not proposing to play the whole thing, and I am proposing to tender the whole thing so it will be available to everyone to look at if they need to. That's what's proposed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I hope there will be some logistic preparations concerning playing of that tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It's time for the break. We'll resume at 11.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, before we start, I have to say that this afternoon -- I'm sorry, this afternoon we'll sit from 3.30 instead of 2.15, because, you know, we should have enough time for lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour, can I say I think the progress is quite good and I'm -- I remain hopeful if we lose an hour we might still be able to do it. So let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, pardon me. Mr. Karavelic, there was just a matter I should have dealt with before the break which I forgot to. I asked you before the break about whether you saw an order from President Izetbegovic concerning the dismissal of Musan Topalovic and Ramiz Delalic, and I'd just like to show you a document now and see whether this is the order we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours we don't have this uploaded, I'm sorry. This is a photocopied document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI 401.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Would you mind just taking the opportunity to look at that quickly and just see whether that's the order that you were referring to earlier on in the cross-examination. Decision, I should say.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I offer that document for tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. It's admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D401.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thanks very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, before the break you indicate -- we had a discussion about certain documents, and I understand you've been kind enough to draft a couple of documents for us. Could I ask, please, did you have the opportunity to draft a rough map of Sarajevo with the units broadly drawn on them?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I managed to do some of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Is it in a position where it mentions the main units surrounding Sarajevo at this stage?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean defending Sarajevo, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I do. That's what I mean. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could that be please be shown how -- I understand that the witness had a chance to draft that on court equipment, and I wonder if that could be displaced, please. Excellent, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: There were two units called the 1st Glorious Brigade and the 2nd Knightly Brigade. Would you mind just indicating where they were based? Perhaps just by -- I'm not sure what the best way to designate those is, but could you indicate where they were? Perhaps before you draw on the map I'll just ask you to indicate verbally where they were. In that map, the 1st Glorious Brigade, whereabouts is that to be found?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the 1st glorious, and this is the 2nd Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. With respect to those two brigades, their engagement on the combat line was sufficiently intense that you couldn't really take units out of Sarajevo to help others from those two units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not 100 per cent but to a large extent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. And although this is very obvious to you we just to have to be very clear in this Court. The 1st glorious and 2nd Knightly Brigades that are referred to there are quite different units to the 1st and 2nd Brigades that are found at the far left-hand end of the map; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And when we refer to the individual Mujo Zulic, he was the commander of the brigade -- the 1st Brigade, that is at the far left-hand end of the map; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that's the one that I'm underlining here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Now, just so that the Tribunal understand a further matter, at the top right-hand of the -- of the map is drawn the 4th Motorised Brigade. Is that the unit that was under the command of Fikret Prevljak?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: When persons travelled through the tunnel underneath the airport, did they then, when they came out, find themselves in the zone of responsibility of Fikret Prevljak and his corps -- and his brigade?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe that in the transcript it should be the 5th Motorised Brigade instead of 4th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I'm not sure about that. The -- perhaps I could clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just because of a question asked by His Honour Judge Liu there, could I just clarify this? The unit at the top right-hand corner of that map, that is the 4th Mechanised Brigade -- the 4th Motorised Brigade commanded by Fikret Prevljak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just on the -- since we discussed rumours, operative information, and gossip that was going around Sarajevo concerning commanders, there was plenty of such rumour, gossip and story-telling about Fikret Prevljak and his supposed criminal activities as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay.
