And in fact, by virtue of Fikret Prevljak's position at the end of the tunnel there, I'm not suggesting that you had concrete facts about him in September 1993, but the rumours were that he had a very major part to play in the smuggling activities of things coming in and out of Sarajevo through the tunnel; is that correct, in terms of those rumours?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: But to get rid of Fikret Prevljak would have required an act of political will which just never happened while you were commander of the 1st Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first part of your question is correct. But by the end of 1994, when I was forming divisions, the operations group or rather the division was formed in the city of Sarajevo, and I had other proposals, but I believe, and I would have to consult some papers, but I believe that he was appointed as commander of that division in the city of Sarajevo and this was not in line with my proposal. So he was promoted basically, and on the occasion of him taking over as the commander of the 4th Motorised Brigade, I was put in a position in which I -- well, since I was not in a position to influence the first part of the decision, then I asked a question about who the new commander for the 4th Motorised Brigade was going to be. Fikret Prevljak, appointed a man that he wanted and he requested it from President Izetbegovic. And that's another occasion where I had serious problems and, in the end, after a longer period of time, perhaps a month, a month of correspondence and all that, I managed to put my principles into practice and the man who was appointed was the one I had suggested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Okay. Now, the last question I have about that map that's on the screen is that there is a unit there marked as "HVO." Now, is it the fact that a unit which had been in the early days of the war an HVO unit still maintained part of the front line against the Republika Srpska forces within Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And what was the name of that particular brigade?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigade of the HVO, initially, at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I offer that for tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There is no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It's admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D402.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The next -- yes. Could that document, although it's been tendered, is it possible for that to be returned to the screen because there has been some data lost. We -- we are using a computer system here, and sometimes things go o wrong. Would you mind just marking again the same marks that you put before? There was an underlining of the -- of Mujo Zulic brigade, there was a line underneath that. There were squares around the 1st Glorious Brigade and 2nd Knightly Brigade and I think you'd also placed a square around Fikret Prevljak's units. Would you mind doing those please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And Could you ask you, having done that, were there any other marks that you put on that map that we've forgotten about? Because they should be the same as before, if possible.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think not. I'm not sure whether previously I underlined the 4th Motorised Brigade, and the rest is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm just asking now for a brief comment about the little try angles that you've put. Do those triangles angles indicate the headquarters of those units marked next to them?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. And where was the Main Staff office?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. I do mean that.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to indicate it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. Thank you very much for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I tender that document? It may be appropriate to tender the original as well, I'm not sure what the mechanics of that are but this is the one we want most but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. But where is the headquarters of the 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours I think it's directly below but we can ask the witness that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Is the 1st Corps headquarters designated below that with the "1K"?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Command of the 1st Corps is what I'm indicating now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: There is just one other matter now - sorry - before we tender that. Are you able to indicate where the Presidency was? Perhaps with a "P" for presidency.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, but in a different colour so as not to confuse anything, the Presidency building was here, right, and I'll mark it with a P.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And if you coloured it in so it was fully black then we could see that it was different to a military type of unit.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, finally I offer that document for tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It's admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D403.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Before my learned friend goes on, before -- I raise this matter in advance. Before the break he indicated that he with would be tendering the transcript of the Zenica meeting and the tape. I've made inquiries over the -- since then. The Prosecution does not have an English translation of the entire Zenica meeting. We have one in B/C/S. We actually requested a translation but because it wasn't on our exhibit list, the request for translation was denied. So we do not have the English translation. So I would very much request a copy of the English translation my copy of the B/C/S is 190 pages long. We certainly couldn't deal with that on the screen if it -- if it were tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's -- it's reasonable. I thought -- Your Honours might recall in relation to this Zenica transcript that the matter was raised with a witness previously, Salko Gusic, who was also present -- present at this meeting, and we don't have a full transcript either. We just have a partial transcript of relevant parts. What my learned friend says is quite right. But I actually believed, and in fact I still do believe now, that I think we gave Ms. Chana a copy of this document at the time of our -- of our partial English transcript. So my learned friend is substantially in the same position we are, although slightly better because he's got the full Bosnian one. We've only got a partial Bosnian one to work from. I don't know how to resolve this matter really, because it -- we don't need to pollute these proceedings by masses of tapes. The Prosecutor of course, is entitled to go to any part of it they want to, and really we are tendering it to make absolutely clear what our submission is about it, that -- namely, that there is no mention of these things on it. That's why. So we have given a copy, but we'll give another copy of what we have and if there is any -- if there is any other common sense way to deal with it, we are very open to suggestions. Would you just excuse me, Your Honour, for one second?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry, I'm just instructed a long time ago there was released in the E-court system. I don't think it's been tendered. What's released in the E-court system has got -- what we are going to hand up now has got blacked-out bits. Those blacked-out bits are comments by Ms. Delalic, who is present in court, because she actually provided the Bosnian transcript from which the English was made, and there are a couple of comments by her in there, which we have noted. In the transcript we are going to hand up now, we've blanked them out, but of course we don't want to interfere with documents so -- anyway, it's -- this is a long-winded process. I'm sorry, Your Honour. Could I just indicate the number when it was released was DD002577. So I understand the Prosecution's position entirely, frankly, and we are somewhat in the same position. But perhaps if we can proceed in the best way we can now to see -- to see what develops in relation to that, and we will provide another copy of this -- of what we have to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Are we going to deal with another chart?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, we are going to deal with the -- with the 1st Corps chart now before we get to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Karavelic, my apologies for that management delay. Now, could we just now come to the next document. Do you have did you have the opportunity in the break to draw a rough chart of the command structure of the 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could that now please be shown on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI 404.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, can I just ask you a couple of questions about the realities of the size of the staff of a corps? How many people did you have in your corps staff? Approximately. I understand not person for person but -- was it 20 or a hundred or 50 or what sort of range?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: 30 to 40, okay. Thank you. And what was the staff of a -- I'll withdraw that. I'll come to some staff sizes later on. What was the normal size of a brigade staff? I mean, bearing in mind they all varied in size, but an average brigade, what sort of size of, in terms of personnel, was their staff?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At any rate, less than a corps. Roughly speaking, up to 15 men, about 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: About 15 in a brigade, and what about at battalion level? Approximately how many might you find in a battalion staff?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the battalion level it's not called "staff." It has a different name but it doesn't really matter but that's the same thing, you're quite right and the number would be some 7, 8, 10, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand. Very well, thanks. And finally, in terms of operative groups or operations groups you've indicated that those groups were temporary formations which, in terms of the hierarchy, stood at some similar sort of position to the permanent type of institution of a division. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: What was the normal size of a -- of a divisional staff? Appreciating that at this time there weren't any divisions but once divisions came into being, what sort of size di the -- was a divisional staff, approximately?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between the corps staff and the brigade staff, we spoke about that a little bit earlier. So it would be an average of about 20 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. As to the operative group, which -- perhaps I should ask you this just to make clear for the transcript. In 1993, there weren't any divisions but there were some operative groups in the Bosnian army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And the staffs of the operative groups were to some degree smaller than those of the division -- the permanent structure of that size; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Even so, however, they -- you would still expect an operative group staff to be larger than that of a brigade, given that an operative group might have one or more brigades under its control; is that an accurate statement?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. And just on that topic of operative groups, if possible, in order to set up an operative group, there needs to be the appointment of a commander of such an operative group; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And because it's at a higher level than a brigade level, that commander has to be appointed with the ultimate authority of the Presidency; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And not only does the commander of the operative group have to be appointed but so, too, do certain officers who go to make up the staff of that operative group, with their functions designated in the order; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And is it also the case that when an operative group is set up, the -- not only the commander of that operative group, but the units that are to be part of that operative group have to be described in the order; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. I'll -- I'll -- I'll -- I'll phrase it another way. When an operative group is established, the units which go to make up that operative group have to be set out in an order effecting the resubordination of those units to that new operative group; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one clarification. When any unit is formed, and this includes the category of an operative group, two orders are written. One is an organisational order, which includes all that you have put in your question, and after that, there is a second personal order appointing people to various duties, including the one of operative group commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand. And it's only when both orders are made that it can be said that the operative group exists; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, according to legal norms, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And in terms of an operative group in the -- in the -- in the current case, you yourself never did hear that -- perhaps before I get to that point about what you heard and what you didn't hear, the normal person to be appointed as commander of a -- of an operative group would be a person -- I'm thinking at the moment of the concrete case of Mr. -- Brigadier Cikotic but an appropriate person to appoint to an operations group would be a person who was somewhat senior to a brigade commander but somewhat junior to a corps commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes, but this doesn't have to be a rule, and it's not always a rule. Two officers of the same rank -- you can have two officers of the same rank. However, the person that holds the higher establishment post is superior to the other one. So it's rank plus function.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Function has more weight than rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And perhaps that's raised another issue that rank and seniority -- sorry, perhaps I'll take a step back. Normally it's the function of -- of the officer which determines who is superior, but is it the fact that sometimes you'll have officers whose function is the same? For example, two brigade commanders? And then perhaps I understand this is perhaps not an expert question but in that situation, seniority and rank will determine who is the superior when the -- when two -- let me just start that question entirely again. We got entirely lost there. I apologise for that. When you have two brigade commanders of equal functional weight, the superiority between them will be determined by reference to their seniority and their rank? Is that an accurate statement?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my understanding, there has been certain things that have being mixed up here. You have two brigade commanders of the same rank and of the same function. This does not happen very often. I think in that case, the superior person would then decide to place one under the other. This is not a usual military rule. If you have two brigade commanders of the same function and the same rank, they would remain that way in any kind of relationship, and in any kind of situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: May I say your answer was helpful even if the question itself was a complete mess, so I thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well, now, I offer that chart that's been drawn for tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It's admitted into the evidence at this stage and I believe that we will instruct the translation section to have it translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D404.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Karavelic, I now want to turn to the Zenica meeting. I'm going to have you shown a tape in a minute. I'll just ask you some general questions first of all. But while I'm asking these questions could just pledges to those in the audiovisual booth that we are going to now ask that videotape number 1 be played, starting at 0.23.03 and go through until 0.24.25. So a length of tape of about a bit over a minute. And, Your Honours, could I just indicate as well that the audio -- that the interpreters' booth is going to make an effort to give a live translation of that. We understand the difficult situation they are in, of course. But they have been provided with a transcript so they are going to help us as best they can for which we are very grateful. After that -- and that's a section which features Mr. Halilovic. And after that comes a section which features the current witness, Mr. Karavelic. Before that's played and I ask that it not be played just yet. I've got a couple of preliminary matters -- questions to ask. Could I just indicate firstly that the tape is -- sorry, that the transcript is Defence document 1509(b), and could I now provide to the Court staff the Bosnian copy and -- the tape itself will be tendered, and that is Defence number 1509(c). Before -- I ask that that not be played straight away. I just have a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Karavelic, do you recall now the Zenica meeting that took place on the 21st and possibly into the 22nd of -- or into the 22nd of August 1993?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, to the best of -- you can't recall whether you were there on the second day of that proceeding or not; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: But it is quite possible that you were, you just don't remember; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, again, to my understanding, you don't have any recollection whether or not you came home from Zenica to Sarajevo via the city of Konjic in the company of Sefer Halilovic and Salko Gusic. Do you remember whether that's the case or not? I'm not suggesting you should remember, but I have to ask you the question.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already given a lot of answers to this question, and I'm a little bit confused about the -- these time periods, immediately after these consultations in Zenica on the 22nd and the days following that. It's possible. However, I cannot claim that 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Look, I'll be quite frank with you about the reason for asking. There is a journalist who gave evidence here named Sefko Hodzic. He said that he saw you and Sefer Halilovic in Konjic on a certain day, and I just wanted to confirm that that's -- with you that that's accurate. If you can't recall, you can't recall. But I think in fairness to all the witnesses I just have to ask you whether you can remember that or not. I take it your answer is, you don't remember it.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I never said that I cannot remember it. I remember that, when I was together with Generals Halilovic and Salko Gusic in front of his corps command in Konjic but there was in the context of being at the at the same time as that famous photograph was made in Jablanica where I am also seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand, okay.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I don't know exactly whether it was that day. I assume that it was, but I don't claim it 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I think you've provided an answer to my question. Thank you. Okay. Well, in any event, while you were at -- at the Zenica meeting, no one discussed Operation Neretva; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And to the best of your recollection, Sefer Halilovic expressed an interest in military operations in the direction of Vitez. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I vaguely seem to remember something about that but I cannot claim to be 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's okay. Look, as I've indicated in court, there is a different reason for tendering this transcript. But, look, what I'll ask you to do now is just have a look at a passage to be played.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly request that a French booth also receives the English copy of the transcript, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. Sorry, Your Honours, we've just had a request from the interpreter's booth that a copy be provided to the French booth as well and we just --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the tape and the transcripts accompanying that will be MFI 405.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Grateful for that. The passage is about to commence now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And Mr. Karavelic, it features Mr. Halilovic speaking and I just ask to you listen to it and then I'll ask you a question about it at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could that now be played, please?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "I would just like to share my opinion with you. And there is room for each of us to reach our own conclusion. Since we still do not have a final answer to this question, according to information from the press, the Presidency in its full composition, without Ganic, has made a decision in Geneva to embark on such a division which is being done now. My opinion in this regard is that we should not dwell on this issue for too long, for the simple reason that the aggressor's goals are to destroy the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina and to destroy the Bosniak Muslim people. Because of that, even through these talks, negotiations, they will offer that part of the territory as much as -- exactly as much territory as would constitute the defeat of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and if this share of the territory is accepted, that would mean a shameful defeat for the army and primarily for the Bosniak Muslim people. In my view, there would be the first step on the way towards our final destruction. Our task is as follows: To reinforce the army, to step up combat readiness, to get stronger, to organise ourselves at all levels, and continue the armed fight. I'm deeply convinced that this will amount to nothing. My proposal is to listen to the corps commanders briefly, to their brief papers, only very brief, identity cards. Please put things into the perspective of problems. This will enable us to come up with solutions together to reach the best possible solutions for us."

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's far as we want that part to be played at this stage. Could that please be stopped now? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if you recall what you said on the tape, but does that accord with your memory of what Sefer Halilovic said at the time?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now I just ask that the witness -- perhaps we just stop there for a moment. Well, that was said. Did you see in that scrambly part of the tape that the -- that the meeting was being chaired by the commander, Commander Delic, on the right of the screen there?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now could we please move to the next point which is 0.44.50? This is going to be a very short part. But -- and it's to go up until 0.45.03, at which point it can stop. I'm really just showing you this for the purpose of reminding you of what you already know, frankly. But I ask that that please be played to the witness. And of course if there is anything more that you wish played of there, you're entitled to ask of that and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: While this is whizzing through, I take it that that speeded-up person there on the screen is you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Could the -- could we just play that short passage now?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] From Lukavica with the forces in Nedjarica by finding Golo Brdo, that would be their objectives at the Igman front or the Bjelasnica front, that part overlaps with the area of responsibility of the 6th Corps. I don't know if we need to go into details here, but when we are talking about the fourth offensive which started in that area on the 1st of July and it started on the 3rd of July in Golo Brdo the objective was at the same time to carry out two Chetnik offensives on two different actions at the same time to bring Sarajevo to a fait accompli. In the first half of July, with a whole bunch of subjective weaknesses, when we are talking about the units of the 1st Corps, I would like to be realistic and objective. It's quite realistic and objective, but subjective weaknesses are first of all command, control, lack of unity, different settling of accounts. To be quite crude, the consequences are that in the first half of July, very quickly, Grebak fell, Delijas fell, Prevoj, Rogoj. The Chetniks went in two axes. One was from Dobro Polje to Prevoj and Rogoj, the second one was from Jahorina via Vis, Grebak, and Delijas. These are these two actions where they managed to break through the lines very quickly with powerful artillery support, and grouping of their forces, specialised infantry units. They broke through those sections with a large use of psychological and propaganda war. These were different methods of work. They did what they did, causing panic, chaos and an exodus of the civilian population and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I might ask that it be stopped there and I'm grateful for that. Although of course, once again, if it's sought by anyone to play further we can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could I just confirm that that was you reporting to the Zenica meeting on the situation that had developed in the area of the 1st Corps as a result of the troubles on Igman?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. And when you mentioned the command and control, the command problems that you mentioned during the course of that, were you referring to the same sort of problems about which you've spoken at length in this Tribunal here?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was just a part of the problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours I offer that -- I know it's been marked. I now offer the tape and the transcript that goes with it for tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just have an inquiry. Our understanding is it's not full tape, that there is a portion missing from it. There is a gap in the tape. It doesn't record the entire proceedings. And the transcript seems to be -- it seems to have piecemeal bits recorded from it. Can I -- can I -- can we ascertain from the Defence whether that is in fact the situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is in fact the situation. The first -- the tape itself has been -- the last part has been cut off by somebody at some stage. Evidence was given by Salko Gusic about that. He was a witness who had been given the opportunity by OTP investigators to look at the whole tape and he could confirm here that he had looked at the whole tape and that he confirmed that the tape had been cut and that a part of the end was missing, and he described what that part was. And he gave clear evidence about all that, upon which the Defence will obviously rely. Now, this witness has not been shown the tape frankly just simply for time purposes here because we know we are rushing to finish. For that purpose. But to answer the Prosecutor's question, yes, the tape was cut, the tape itself is clearly incomplete and has been confirmed as such. And furthermore, the transcript that we've offered to tender here is only parts of the tape. It's only highlights of it, parts of it, as my friend says it's many, many pages long, many hours long. The Tribunal doesn't really need to sit here unless, of course, if it assist a party's case to ask you to, then, of course, that's open. We don't ask you to do that because we are simply tendering it to show that there is no evidence at all of the discussions which are alleged in the indictment and may be alleged by a witness, depending on what they say. That's why we are tendering it to show it's -- it's really what is not said rather than what is said that we are interested in this tape.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that the second part of the tape was simultaneous translation, and there was no transcript of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the interpreters have just pointed out, for which, I'm grateful that when that translation took place, they didn't have a transcript from us. I must say, I thought that the part that I thought I was getting was a little bit different to what came, although the relevant information came, in any event, so it's -- from the Defence point of view. However, the interpreters are entitled to be covered by this. We thought we had given the transcript, but obviously not. Now, that's what I can offer about the transcript. I'm not sure now what the Prosecution's position is. Do they oppose us or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's not a position of opposing it. The Defence is proposing to tender portions of the transcript. Our concern is that there is an entire B/C/S transcript of 190 pages. Hour concern is the selective tendering of portions, and I understand it is to be linked at some later point to a submission that Neretva isn't mentioned on the part of the tape that we do have. This English transcript won't -- of course won't prove that because it's only selective portions. If the Defence -- if my learned colleague could just perhaps elaborate a little bit on that, it may -- it may overcome our concerns about the selective tendering or the highlighted portions. I don't quite understand at the moment the purpose of tendering highlighted portions in an attempt to show that Neretva wasn't discussed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I can -- I can indicate that, Your Honour. In the first instance, the tape itself is being tendered, and this is regardless of the transcript at all, to show that there is no mention of the things that are said in the indictment, that are supposed to have happened at Zenica. At least according to the Prosecutor's case. So we tender the tape itself to prove that. We do that against a background where the Prosecutors have this tape already, put it in full in their investigations to a witness, Mr. Gusic, who was called here, through whom they did not seek to tender that tape. And you can draw a clear inference from that that they know very well there is no mention at all of these matters on that tape. Otherwise, they would have tendered it in evidence. But however to make crystal clear that the Defence wants to underline that fact, so we are tendering the tape. If the Prosecution won't do it, we can't force them to. But we are going to do it, because we want there to be no doubt at all that no such thing happened. As to the editing of the tape at the end, we don't know who did it. And if an appropriate witness comes along we will grill them about that question. If they come along. So that's -- that's that side. However, as to the transcript, there are parts of the tape that may be of interest. For example, words said by the late Arif Pasalic about the plot of the 4th Corps down in Mostar. Now, some of these were put in general terms to the witness Gusic, he agreed with some, couldn't remember others and gave comments in general terms. The court might recall, I actually put parts of the transcript to him. I'm sure you don't recall the actual incident, but I did put it to him. So his subjective concerns play well be matters of background relevance to this Tribunal because it's said that the situation in Mostar was very bad and part of that is that Arif Pasalic, the commander, was saying at the Zenica meeting that it was very bad. Likewise, Commander Gusic made some complaints about the difficulties he faced and you'll recall one thing you may recall because it could have relevance was some of the smaller units were not complying with the line of command and control and the 6th Corps. The "crni Labudovi," that's the Black Swans Unit, was one. The "Akrepi" was another unit, and other units like that were mentioned. So that the subjective concerns of the individual commander at that meeting can shed some light. It is only background, but it's -- it can show some light. And finally, the Prosecutor tendered into evidence a document which we have been calling the Zenica conclusions. That's a document dated the 29th of August, and that document is relevant because it shows if you like what Rasim Delic thought had emerged from that meeting and what action he proposed to take at a very high level, it has to be stressed, about that. For those reasons, therefore, the Defence has produced the transcript of those parts which we thought seemed to be of relevance, are capable of being of relevance. We don't have the resources to have the whole thing transcribed. We just don't have it. And what we submit is it would not help this Tribunal in any way to have the whole thing transcribed unless you wish to here about the Bosnian air force and other topics or the situation in the Bihac area or in Gorazde and other places like that. Now I don't, frankly, know myself what's on some of the parts of the tape. If it is to the Prosecutor's advantage to play those things, one would have thought that they would have done it in their own case. They've got this tape. For that reason, to assist the Tribunal, I do still seek to tender that tape. The tape it really the evidence, not the transcript. The transcript is just there to help with the tape. It's the tape that is evidence. If the transcript's wrong, then it's not to be relied upon. You've got a tape there. If the Prosecution wants to assist you by pointing out parts of the tape which are wrong, well, we are happy and they can, of course they can do that. But for that reason we submit that it should be submitted and it should be received just as an aid to the Tribunal like transcripts normally are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We don't object to the tape now, but my query was actually about the transcript. Can the Defence link the portions of the transcript they seek to tender with the days? There is a date of the 221st and the 22nd of August 1995. This witness's evidence in chief was he cannot remember whether he attended on both days. We are interested in whether the transcript can be linked to the two separate days on which the meeting was said to occur. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I can't -- I can't do it through this witness. I can't do it through this witness because he doesn't remember. There is another witness coming who was present at that -- well, when I say "coming," there is another witness on the list, named -- who was there. And he might know. We might ask him questions. At the moment, all we have is -- is a tape that was cut at some stage, but Your Honours what we can do, of course, is -- Ms. Delalic was the person who produced there. I can easily ask her to say at what -- which of the tapes are used and at what point. We can provide that information to the Prosecutors if they haven't had a chance to look at that tape in the last ten months or so, and, Your Honour, we will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Generally speaking, I believe that there is no problem for the tape as well as for the transcript to be admitted into the evidence. And the selective tendering and admission is possible, and we have done that especially concerning of some very thick books in the past. So the tape and the transcript are admitted into the evidence at this stage. Of course, in the future, if we have other witnesses who participated in this meeting, they could also give some evidence concerning some details. It is so decided.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The Court deputy will pronounce the number of the two.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 405, D405.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thanks very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. We now turn to the -- the combat activities that took place down in the Neretva valley early in September of 1993. And I just want to ask you a couple of very general introductory questions. The first of those questions is: That you yourself had absolutely nothing to do with those -- those combat activities beyond complying with an order from Sefer Halilovic to send down some units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I just want to get some specifics about that. In some ways it's repetitious but I just need to go through it. You, yourself, did not attend any planning meetings concerning combat operations in that area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Nor did you meet with Suljevic, Bilajac, and Karic concerning any specific combat operations in the Neretva valley; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You were familiar with the concerns that commander Arif Pasalic had for his troops and civilians in Mostar but you didn't discuss combat -- specific combat operations to relieve Mostar with him either; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You didn't discuss specific combat operations with Sefer Halilovic or with Rasim Delic in the Neretva valley; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: At the time, whether all this was going on, you did not see that inspection team order dated the 30th of the 8th about which we have had some evidence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Nor did you see the map which has been shown to you in evidence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Nor did you see any order appointing Sefer Halilovic as the commander of any operations group; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Nor did you see any order appointing Sefer Halilovic as the commander of anything at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Nor did you hear the name "Operation Neretva" prior to the departure of your troops -- I say "your troops," of the troops that were taken out of your unit down to Herzegovina; is that true?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Nor did you see any order creating an IKM in Jablanica or indeed in Donja Jablanica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Nor did you see any order referring to an operation called "Operation Neretva," or, to use the Prosecution's phrase, "Operation Neretva 93"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't remember seeing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And apart from the order shown to you by the Prosecution and dated the 15th of September 1993, in which Sefer Halilovic appears to issue certain instructions and under the heading of an order, you did not see any other document that was a combat order by Sefer Halilovic relating to that period; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only saw those documents upon my arrival to The Hague now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And -- nor did you see any report from combat troops to Sefer Halilovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen the reports from the 9th and the 10th Brigades and as to the 2nd Motorised Battalion, it is possible I might have seen it, but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. But as to the 2nd Independent Battalion, the report that you saw -- the one that you think you might have seen, is that the document that they showed you here that you've looked at here, dated the 25th of -- of September 1993?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's that document. I don't really know if it's the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's okay but in relation to that document -- yes, I understand, sorry, pardon me. I understand your answer. Okay. Now, okay. Just pardon me a second. All right. And just further to those questions, that I've asked you, the situation you were facing in Sarajevo -- I'll put a proposition you tell me if I'm right or wrong. The situation was that on every day there would be combat activities of some sort on the perimeter of Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And in particular, in the zone of engagement of the 1st Glorious Brigade and the 2nd Knightly Brigade, there was very common and heavy fighting most of the time, is that correct? In the area of [inaudible]?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. And although it might be a short answer and a short answer which doesn't capture the full situation, is the fact this: You were very busy for every minute that you were awake trying to defend Sarajevo and also your area of responsibility outside Sarajevo on the other side of the tunnel, on Igman; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. And sometimes they were totally lost in all that occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And in that context, you had no competence and no reason to be discussing with Rasim Delic, or with Sefer Halilovic, the combat details of whatever was going to happen down in the Neretva valley; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And so you yourself cannot say what power, what nature of power and what degree of power, commander Delic actually gave to Sefer Halilovic with respect to the combat activities in the Neretva valley; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'll go to the details of these documents a little bit later on but broadly speaking, the order of the 30th of the 8th, that's the inspection team order, does not on its own face answer the question of whether or not Sefer Halilovic had a command power over the units during the combat activities in Operation Neretva, but that that document is quite ambiguous on that point. Do you agree with that proposition?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, quite a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And turning to the map that you were shown here, once again, as you've pointed out, the map, you would say, is ambiguous on the question of who had command power in relation to combat activities in the Neretva valley and also the extent of any such command power. Is that an accurate proposition?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is less than clear. What do you want me to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, when the question is less than clear, you points it out to me and then I'll ask you a proper question. That's the way we handle that situation. What I'm putting to you is simply by looking at the map, you can't determine who was in command of combat activities in the Neretva valley in September of 1993, is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm a professional soldier, and on the basis of a short yes or no answer, I can't really deal with that question because it wouldn't be sufficient. In replying to one of the previous questions I did already point out that this topographic map that had been shown here and we have a copy here, that that map in itself is not a complete document covering all the combat activities in full. So you may perhaps derive the answer to your question from this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Is another way of -- perhaps another way of asking the question is the map is not sufficiently complete documentation on which to answer that question? Is that a fair way to put the proposition?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is a bit better now, yes, that's it, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Okay. Well -- and again I'm dealing at a very high level of generality here but I'm putting perhaps the high level propositions. The crucial question, I suggest to you, is one that you're not in a position to answer from your own knowledge, and that is: What powers did Rasim Delic actually give to Sefer Halilovic, and/or other people, with respect to combat activities in the Neretva valley? Do you agree that's the appropriate question to ask and do you agree that you're not able to answer it from your own knowledge?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've -- I commented yesterday on the order of the 30th of August, which was submitted to General Halilovic by Rasim Delic and about the contents of that order. And I commented the way I did. Those parts that refer to the content. But what you're now referring to and the question that you seem to be putting, yes, by all means, but what's put in writing is one hand, is on one hand, but the right of any superior officer is always to have the absolute right to issue orders in writing, but also to issue oral orders. That's their absolute right as well. And I do totally agree with you, it is a matter of relationship and the type of communication between Rasim Delic and Sefer Halilovic. It is extremely difficult for me to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Certainly. Very well, I'm now going to turn to the order of the 30th of the 8th itself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well if you're going to details, maybe this is a proper time for to us have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I think we'll have 30 minutes' break and we'll resume at 10 minutes to 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There are just two -- two other matters that I neglected to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Karavelic, there are just two matters there that I forgot about. One of them concerns the ending of the tape of Zenica. I should ask you this: Before today, have you ever been shown that Zenica tape?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of those who -- well, perhaps the key, or rather if I'm not mistaken, two years ago, following a request from somebody from the Prosecution, at the Nedzarici department in Sarajevo, I tried to get these cassettes with the help of some other people. We made a special effort and we managed to get the cassettes that you are referring to. We were told straight away, and this is precisely what you're referring to, we were told about the missing third cassette, or about a missing end to the film representing that meeting. But in my talks with all these people and my conversation with the cameraman who actually made the tape, and I think at the moment he works in Zenica, or I don't know whether he works for radio or television, I'm not sure, but he did say something along the lines that there may not be a tape at all, because there was an interruption there. As to whether his memories were not too -- not all that will clear, I don't know. This is just a minor contribution, for what it's worth, in this entire situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, no. I'm grateful for the indication, but what I might do is well -- perhaps --

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I've never seen the missing bit that you're referring to. I do apologise for not answering your question properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It's okay. But the question is now: Did you view the tapes that they -- that you were provided with -- sorry, perhaps I should ask: Did you get a chance to view the tapes that you sought?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In Sarajevo, I went through -- there are two tapes, I think, if I remember correctly, and I viewed them in their entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just going to show you the end of the tapes and I'll ask you if that accords with your memory in just one second but before I do that, apart from the cutoff at the end, there were no apparent breaks or pieces of editing which you could see within the tape that you viewed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think not. As far as I'm concerned, these are very realistic, truthful, objective pictures, the way I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'm just going to show you the end of the tape and ask you if the tape that you saw cut out and ended in the same way that the tape you're about to look at now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: So could that please be played?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps unless there is something we don't know about, perhaps it could be stopped there. We are grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Did the tape that you saw in Sarajevo cut out at the same point, to the best of your memory, as the one here?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it did. Although if I may comment briefly, my opinion is that this somewhat longer bit at the end of the second tape, indicates that the meeting had basically already been completed but some extra conversation is continuing at the tail end of that meeting whereby people are asking questions and commenting on less essential matters. So the way I see it, it is highly probable that this is the end of the tape because it was not felt that any further tapes would be necessary. But I can't say that I'm 100 per cent sure of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Who was the person who was speaking at the end of that particular tape, to the best of your recollection? When the tape cut off, who was that man speaking?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one to the right, the one that I've just seen, was Rasim Delic, the Staff Commander of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, and the other person who was in the main part of the screen was the accused man here, Sefer Halilovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Thank you. Now just excuse me a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, that brings me to the second matter. Your Honours, I call and the Prosecutors to provide, please, a copy of the complete unadulterated tape that they have in their possession and any translations of that which may chance to exist, to be provided to the Defence as soon as possible, please, because the uninterrupted nature of that tape is a matter of significance in our case. We think it's shown, but we don't want there to be any doubt about it so I ask the Prosecutors to provide that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it's not in the materials of the disclosure before?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, we believe that it may be in the -- what's called the "electronic discovery suite" which is a vast mine of information, but I just want to be clear that what is in there is indeed that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Anybody in the Prosecution in the position to answer this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No. Not when it's, to use Mr. Morrissey's words, sprung on us like this in the middle of trial, no. But we'll look into it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It's really the video that's the -- the significant part, what the Prosecution have there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Anyway, thank you again, Mr. Karavelic, for that. Now, I just want to come now to the -- to some details about -- about how it was that Sefer Halilovic came to send you that order which you complied with and obeyed, which is really your only involvement in this case at all. Now, you were aware -- let me just -- I'll just go to Zenica. Zenica was effectively a chance for all the corps commanders to meet with commander Delic and the Main Staff in order to consider the future direction of the war at a very high and general level, is that an accurate way to put it?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That gathering was probably aimed at -- well, I don't know whether prior to that meeting General Delic had any opportunity to bring together all the corps commanders except for the 5th Corps commander in order to have this sort of meeting, and, yes, basically we can say that you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And after the Zenica conference, on the 29th of August, a document was issued under the hand of commander Delic called "conclusions and tasks."

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Exhibit 109, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: What's going to be shown to you now is a document that was tendered here earlier on in the trial and I'll just ask you for some comments on that document when it comes up. This is quite a lengthy document that's here but just looking at the first page of it, are you able to comment on whether you are familiar with the document? In other words, whether a copy of this was provided to you at some stage by commander Delic?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. And I am familiar with the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Oh, good. Okay. Well could we please go and on the electronic version could we go to the part headed Roman numeral II, tasks, I think it might be two or three pages into the document. I just like you to -- you don't have to do it in any great detail but just to be fair to you just to refresh your memory as to some of the tasks that were issued by Commander Delic arising out of the -- the Zenica meeting. Do you notice that under the heading of tasks, there are a number of individual tasks, which are at a high level of generality, if you like? They are not concerned with -- with specific battles but they are concerned with high level sort of matters concerning education and so on, each one is different of course, but do you agree with that generally speaking, that those tasks that are issued are quite high-level ones?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, one -- could I ask you to direct your attention to number 9, please? With respect to number 9, that seems to get a little more specific than some of the others, but is it the fact that there was a general problem throughout the army, and in particular with respect to the 6th Corps, concerning smaller units which had yet to find a secure place within the line of command and control of the individual corps? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I just want to ask you a specific question about the Zulfikar unit now seeing that it's mentioned there. The Zulfikar unit was a unit which took part in the very desperate struggles of the army throughout 1993, including on Igman; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Is it fair to say -- to describe the Zulfikar unit this way: Sometimes it was in the line of command and control and sometimes it just wasn't? And perhaps you might --

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I can say yes, but this was not within my jurisdiction, so I don't know what that unit -- what the relationship of that unit was to my superiors, but it's probably the way you said in the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand. I'll keep the questions just within what you know, if I can. With respect to the Zulfikar unit, to your knowledge, was that unit a unit which, at least on many occasions, was directly subordinated to the Main Staff rather than being subordinated to a corps?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely. It wasn't subordinated to the 1st Corps at least. It's possible that it was subordinated to others. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Tell me if you remember this, the answer to this question. You may or may not. What -- is it your recollection that the Zulfikar unit was the subject of a number of attempts to place it within the line of command and control of a particular corps, but that that unit did not cooperate with being placed within the control and command of a particular corps, whether that be the 6th Corps or some other corps? Do you remember any such proposition as the one I've put to you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And -- very well. Now, just returning to this document at paragraph 9, the other units described there were similar, smaller units, one might say, popular units with commanders popularly appointed, is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And on the face of this, what Commander Delic was trying to achieve was just one more step in the gradual process of bringing the whole army under a single line of command and control. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Just excuse me a second. In general terms, I won't take you through every word of it just to prove a simple point but do you agree that in that document there, there is no reference to the Operation Neretva or to the appointment of Sefer Halilovic to any command position or indeed to any specific operation in the Neretva valley whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And that document is completely consistent with what you saw and heard at the Zenica conference that you attended; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to say that it's so, 100 per cent, but for the most part, yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Thank you. Okay. Well, I've asked you about Zenica. I've asked you about this particular note. Now I just want to show you to another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the -- I'm sorry, this is a document -- sorry, just pardon me, Your Honour. Just excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours we may have left this off the list of documents that we uploaded. It's not on the list. Sorry, would you just excuse us for a moment? We will provide you with the D numbers in any event. Thank you. Your Honours, could I just indicate and apologise, there has been significant slashing of the -- of the list here, and extra lists have been produced at short notice. The fault is mine not those of anyone else in the team. Okay. Could the witness please be shown document DD000099? Your Honours, a copy of this will be provided to the Prosecutors, but it's a pretty short document in any event. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: This is a letter that's going to be shown to you and I'll just ask you to read it and then I'll ask you some questions about it. Mr. Karavelic, could I just ask, while that's being done, do you have that document yet on the screen or not? Because we don't. We are getting there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter doesn't know whether the witness said yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The answer was no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: But while that's being done, let me just ask you another question, perhaps not to waste all the time. You were familiar with -- with some staff officers, Zicro Suljevic, Rifat Bilajac, and Vehbija Karic during your time as commander of the 1st Corps; is that correct? ?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I just have a question about Vehbija Karic. So far as you were aware, he was a married man who had married a person of Croatian ethnicity; is that correct? His wife was Croatian by background?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so but I'm not 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. Okay. The document that I wanted is now on the screen. And if you wouldn't mind just looking at that -- look at the date of it, which is -- it's dated Jablanica the 1st of September, and look at who it's directed to. And then look at the contents, and I'll ask you -- I'll ask you whether you've seen it before and then I'll ask you to comment on some of the things that are contained in it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI 406.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, among the thousands of documents that you may have seen over time, I suppose I have to ask you this very clearly, do you recall whether you've seen this document before or not?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I've seen it before. I'm seeing it for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, in that event, I'll just ask to you to note certain of the characteristics of it. Does this appear to be a -- at least on the face of it, a document sent from Jablanica by the three individuals at the bottom, just excuse me a moment, sorry, Zicro, Rifat, and Vehbija, a document sent from there to the commander of the Supreme Command Staff, namely Rasim Delic?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. It makes reference -- this document makes reference to a proposal, and what I want to do is ask you whether you recall anything about this proposal that was, at least on the face of this document, current, at -- on the 1st of September 1993. It says here, "we did not know" -- down at the bottom, it's at -- very low down on the page. "We do not know if the proposal that we have sent to use units from Sarajevo and the 3rd Corps met with approval." Now I just want to ask you, from your own memory, did you know about or do you remember anything about a proposal sent by these three individuals to Commander Delic concerning the use of -- I'm just quoting in general terms -- units from Sarajevo and also from the 3rd Corps? I just ask you: What's your recollection, if any, about that topic?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. It's very hard for me to say anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Let me but some questions about what you were doing at that time. On -- at the end of August and at the start of September -- I began to ask you about this before and then we changed streams. At the end of August and at the start of September, although the Igman situation had stabilised to some extent, you were still very concerned about the security of Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And the very last thing you wanted, even if -- I'm sorry, I'll put that in a more formal way I apologise. Although of course you would comply with orders you received, you did not want to give up units from your defence if you didn't positively have to give them up. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely. And this links on to your previous question. For example, if the situation in Igman deteriorated and the aggressor had some successes would mean that Sarajevo would be under a second ring of siege, which would ultimately lead to the death of Sarajevo, because it would be short of food, water, ammunition for combat and so on. So in a way, a good or a bad situation at Igman would reflect equally on Sarajevo. Secondly, in the course of 1993, the aggressor was constantly conducting combat operations vis-a-vis the town so it was a danger every day that the aggressor could enter the town and that the town could fall as a result. And this was always a reflection of the situation at Igman, and that's the reason why I did what I did, and in a way, it's also the answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And I appreciate the answer. Well, because of that pressure that you were under, do you -- in terms of any discussions sorry I'll take a step back. You indicated a memory that you had of a conversation with Sefer Halilovic, possibly a telephone conversation, in which you discussed some troops -- the possibility of troops being sent down to Herzegovina to help in combat activities there. And what I want to ask you is this: Are you able to comment on the possibility that these inspection team members, Zulic, Bilajac, and Karic, did in fact have a conversation with commander Delic on the topic of getting extra units from Sarajevo and also from the 3rd Corps? Can you comment on that or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I mean, that's really speculative. It goes a little bit too far in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Unless there is some basis for you to ask this question, otherwise, this question is not allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour the basis would be: If he remembers it, he remembers it; and if he doesn't, he doesn't. And that will be -- if he doesn't remember, it's the ends. If he remembers it, I'll ask him what he remembers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The question is not whether he remembers or not. The question is whether he knew or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Ah, well to the extent of a difference Your Honour I'll certainly ask it this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Do you remember whether there was such discussions going on between Commander Delic and the three inspection team members, Suljevic, Bilajac, and Karic, exploring the possibility of getting some extra units from Sarajevo and possibly the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember anything like that specifically but this document indicates something like that, and we can see from it that these talks had taken place, these discussions. I don't know what else to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's okay. You just say what you can remember and that's what you're being asked. Going further from that, did Sefer Halilovic in the conversation with you, do you recall whether he made any reference to this matter, in other words, that Vehbija Karic, and Suljevic, and Bilajac had already discussed this matter with Rasim Delic and canvassed the possibility of taking some of your troops?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did speak with him, and General Sefer Halilovic spoke to me about the possibility of taking units from the 1st Corps, but I don't remember us talking about whether Zicro, Rifat, and Vehbija talked with General Delic or not. This was beyond my area. I could have heard or found out about it quite by coincidence, but it was not a part of my chain, so I really didn't know regardless of whether it did happen or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And well let me just ask you then some other questions about -- about what Sefer Halilovic said. Do you -- you indicated when we asked you about -- when you were asked by my learned friend, Mr. Re, and me about this conversation, you indicate add general memory rather than word-for-word memory. Is that a fair way to put the situation in terms of that telephone conversation?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Is it possible that Sefer Halilovic in that conversation asked you whether you'd be prepared to provide units from the 1 Glorious Brigade and the 2nd Knightly Brigade for his purposes down in Herzegovina? In other words, is it possible that he asked you for those units?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Again it's the same objection. I mean, anything is possible. The real question should be: Did he or do you recall him asking you that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, maybe the form of the question is not so proper, but generally speaking this kind of question is allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'll put the question more directly to your memory about it. Do you remember whether or not Sefer Halilovic made that inquiry of you during that conversation?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's really hard to say. I would rather say that I really don't remember. I don't remember that units were mentioned at all. Actually units were discussed, but I don't remember that specific units were mentioned. I don't think that they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, just in terms of the concrete situation facing the 1st Glorious Brigade and the 2nd Knightly Brigade, who had you been asked to release them, what were the relevant factors that would have determined your answer about those two in terms of their obligations on the front line?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I decided about that as the commander of the 1st Corps. In making my decision, I put the significance of a certain unit at a given point in time as the most important thing while I was making my decision, and we are talking about the glorious and the knightly units, because they had a very important part, and they bore the heaviest burden in the defence of Sarajevo. And I decided -- I would be reluctant to decide to send units from those brigades anywhere, or I wouldn't do it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, now, in terms of fighting abilities, it was perfectly sensible for Sefer Halilovic to ask for units of the 9th and the 10th to be provided to him for combat operations down in Herzegovina, in the order which he ultimately sent you; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He could have done that, absolutely. He had the right to do that. And in my opinion, this does not run counter to anything in terms of my own professional military opinion. At the same time, this could have been some other unit also.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And the fact is that when those units were chosen to go down and fight, and when you said goodbye to the 9th Brigade in particular, never for one second did it occur to you these people might commit atrocities against civilians; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: What you expected from those units was that they would behave with honour and seek to bring about conclusions consistent with the platform of the Presidency and the purposes of the army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And, of course, if you personally as a professional commander had have had any thoughts that there was danger like that, and I'm not suggesting for one second you should have had such thoughts, but if you had have any such thoughts you would have made it clear, "Don't take these units"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without any doubt, and to the least possible degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
