utterances.text: And I suppose just to follow that up, you knew of course when they were being dispatched that they were going to be sent to fight in Herzegovina against the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, Sarajevo was a town that had a very mixed population of different people of different ethnic backgrounds at the time of the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. In the corps command, during 1992 and 1993, my morale assistant was a Serb by the name of Rajko Mihajlovic. In my corps, the legal affairs assistant, from day one to the last day of the war, throughout the whole four years of the war, I had an assistant whose name was Zlatko Petrovic, and he's a minister today in one of the ministries in the Sarajevo canton. The number one man in the artillery of the corps was a Croat named Miro Grbavac. The commander of a unit which reported to the corps command, it was a light artillery and anti-aircraft defence unit, was a Croat by the name of Darvin Lisica, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And within the city of Sarajevo, Bosniak Muslims who lived there often lived side by side with their Croatian neighbours who also stayed and lived in Sarajevo and joined the struggle; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's what you were actually fighting to protect, that sort of neighbourly relations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was something very basic, and it was the foundations of the future Bosnia-Herzegovina that I was fighting for, and I believe 100 per cent that General Halilovic also fought for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And in concrete terms, in the city of Sarajevo, that meant that -- okay, could I just ask you this: When soldiers finished on the line, finished their line duty in Sarajevo and went off duty, did they go and live in big, organised barracks rooms like a regular army or did they go home to their own homes in Stari Grad or elsewhere? What was the general practice for soldiers off duty there?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Corps, as I said, in 1993, numbered somewhere around 75.000 soldiers. Even at peacetime, you can't provide housing for such large numbers of soldiers, not to mention a wartime in Sarajevo when two-thirds of overall infrastructure was either torched, destroyed, and totally useless. So the conclusion is that out of the entire number of soldiers, about 40.000 in the city of Sarajevo where the 1st Corps is concerned, perhaps -- I'm just going to give you one figure. Perhaps 5.000 or 6.000 soldiers had some sort of housing, but even that was improvised housing in cellars and parts of some buildings. Everybody else, and all that housing was provided for those units and those soldiers who had to be in a certain state of preparedness, who had to be ready to intervene within a quarter of an hour if there was a problem along the defence lines of the city of Sarajevo. They had to rush out to the front lines and start fighting straight away, in case there was a problem with those defence lines. Everybody else was either on the defence lines or, if not, they were at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Thank you for that. One of the things I wanted to find out from you is -- is this: It was pretty common just for Bosniak soldiers to live next door to their Croat neighbours in peace in the city of Sarajevo, to your understanding; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the selection of billeting facilities for the troops that were sent down to Herzegovina, first of all, the selection of those billeting facilities had absolutely nothing to do with you personally; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what facilities you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Pardon me. What I'm talking about is where the -- where the soldiers from the 9th and 10th Brigade and 2nd Independent Battalion who were sent out of Sarajevo by you and went down to Herzegovina, those soldiers had to be billeted somewhere and the question is: You had nothing to do with the selection of the place where they were billeted; is that correct? You as corps commander just had nothing to do with any such thing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And in the concrete case of course these troops were not under your control once they left Sarajevo, and I understand that, but in any event, the billeting of 200 troops or so is not a matter that the corps commander would normally concern himself with, even if they were in your zone; is that correct? That would be a matter for somebody lower down the chain; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in the event that -- I understand you don't -- you weren't involved in what happened down there but I just have to ask you this as a -- in the event that these units were -- were subordinated, or at least ordered to be subordinated or suggested to be subordinated, to the unit of Zulfikar Alispago, then, of course, it fell to local commander -- I withdraw that because it's a hypothetical. You can't comment on it. I'll deal with it in a different way. In the case of units that are sent down it on a mission like that, units let's say 200 soldiers strong, approximately, it would fall to the local commander at a company or possibly battalion level to organise accommodation for those troops; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And in assessing where to place particular troops, the local commander would have to take into account all of his local knowledge to determine what was the appropriate place to put those troops; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: So that that commander would have to consider, first of all, what was the available range of choices of places to put such troops; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Then he'd have to consider whether the units that he was accommodating had any special dislike for the local population. For example, a history of anti-Croat behaviour; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely. That was one in a series of steps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Of course. And I'm just going through a number of these -- these steps now. Then he would have to consider whether or not there was water nearby for the troops to drink and a suitable place for a communications centre to be established?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely. Those elements and many others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, there are a whole host of matters that have to be taken into account by the local commander in determining those matters. But, in fact, let me just ask you: Are you aware of whether or not in Jablanica and Grabovica, in early September 1993, whether there was a big influx of refugees taking up a lot of space in those -- in that -- in those two places?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, and as far as I know, from many sources, the media or sources of information coming from the political and military leaders, with regard to those matters and the state of affairs down in the valley of Neretva, there was a great deal of confusion. It was chaotic and there was a huge number of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: So -- now if a commander was given -- where a commander is given the opportunity to billet, where a commander was given an opportunity to billet -- to billet a mixed force of Bosnian army soldiers, by which I mean a mixed force, including Bosniaks, Croats, and Serbs, where a commander was given the opportunity to billet such soldiers in a village populated by old and relatively friendly Croatian villagers, then if the other options were limited, then it's perfectly open to such a commander to make that decision to put them there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And of course, in that situation, if such a mixed unit is billeted with those old Croat civilians, of course a staff unit should go and see if the troops are settling in and if everything is under control and conditions are friendly; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, I've drifted a bit forward into the world of the things that actually happened there and I need to -- need to come and -- come back to where we were. Anyway you've indicated already that as to this document with Vehbija, Zicro, and Rifat, you can't recall seeing it, and you've indicated what you can remember about the conversation with Sefer Halilovic. Soon after that, you got a -- you got a -- on the 2nd of September, you got an order from Sefer Halilovic to please -- and then could the witness please be shown Exhibit - I'm sorry, just excuse me - as to that document of -- with Rifat, Zicro, and Vehbija, I offer that document for tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It's admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D406.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I understand it's time for the break. So could we break now and continue your cross-examination in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And we'll resume at 3.30 in the same courtroom. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.45 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey. Are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Karavelic. We are just going to spend -- I'm going to ask you some questions for the next 15 minutes or so concerning some limited aspects of military theory. Some of this might be very basic for you but it's -- it helps the Court to have some of it on the record so I'm going to show you a couple of documents I'll ask you for brief comments on it, and you feel free to comment, if you feel as if you're being put in a funny position by being shown part of a document you should tell us that because we may not know. So -- but in any event, having said that -- just excuse me one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours I'm going to now put to the witness some parts of a book with a title in English, "The Theory of Military Control." Can I indicate that some of this -- most of this was put to the witness Selmo Cikotic who gave evidence a month or so ago, and because -- it's up loaded into the system in Bosnian language but not in English but, however, we've photocopied the transcript of the hearing of Mr. Cikotic to an English version can be before the Tribunal and the Prosecutors as well, of course, so I just ask that this be distributed now and I would ask meanwhile that MFI 195 be displayed on the screen. That's in Bosnian. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, on the screen, there is a document I'm going to show you, it's computerised, but it's -- it's title is the "The Theory of Military Control. " May I just ask you first of all, are you familiar with that particular book?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Do you have that on the screen in front of you there or not?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I'm not in any way attempting to set an exam, I can assure you I'm not fitted to do that, but I just want to put certain parts of it to you and could the witness please be shown page 2 of that document, as it is uploaded and Mr. Karavelic you'll have in front of you a page that has a heading, "Two, obnas rukovodjenje i komanovanje. [phoen]" Do you see that heading?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, the second paragraph down concerns a definition of the process of -- just excuse me one moment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, on page 73 of the transcript at line 7, the passage that I'm going to put to the witness is to be found. It's the same passage that I put to Mr. Cikotic long ago at line 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well, if you just read that passage and I'll read at the same time from the transcript here, "the military dictionary defines command as the function of control in the armed forces with the interpretation of the right of officers to make decisions. It is important to say that only persons authorised by law, regulations and rules are authorised to command and not other command staffs or some other control structures." Now, is that an accurate -- or, sorry, does that quotation accurately reflect military doctrine as it was or as it was supposed to be in the Bosnian army in 1993?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, they did not have their own special military doctrine. They had taken over the military doctrine of the JNA. In the case of the first part of this quote, the one that you've just read out, yesterday or the day before, I did say word for word, as it were, that command is a part of control, an integral part of control. That's what I said. So, for example, the first sentence of this quote confirms that, but it says at the same time that command and control are things that go hand in hand, and they can be separated. It's not impossible. But they normally go together. And the second part of the quote, generally speaking, I would tend to agree, but if we were to ask a whole series of questions, because there is a rather general statement, you know, so at one point it says, "command can be carried out only by people entitled to do so by law," and the question arises: Who are these people entitled to do that? And then the rules and regulations, what rules? What regulations? Command staff or some other sort of control structure. With reference to this part of the sentence, and this is my view, the command is not in command. It is quite right. I mean, when it comes to the 1st Corps, the command of the 1st Corps commands the corps. But if we look at it on the basis of this part of your quote, the commander of the 1st Corps is the person who has the exclusive right to command the 1st Corps. And the entire command of the corps depends on him, is accountable to him. In the same way the entire staff of the Supreme Command is accountable to the Supreme Command Staff Commander. And so what you are saying here is absolutely correct. The command of the staff or any other structure are not entitled to command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I'm grateful for that and I just want to ask for a little further explanation arising from this quote, perhaps stepping outside it slightly, but I want to put the question to you. At the high level, say, at the corps level or even higher, at the General Staff or Main Staff level, do -- does a Chief of Staff exercise some -- some parts of rukovodjenje, of the general function of control, without actually exercising command powers? In other words, do chiefs of staff participate with coordination, planning and the other four parts of the control process but not in the command process unless they have specific authority to do so? Would you comment on that, place?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By putting this question, you've actually explained it very nicely. Your very question in itself provides us with an answer. So roughly speaking that's the way it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You have no idea how relieved I am, Mr. Karavelic. I'm sorry, I do struggle with these concepts myself from time to time. But so, it's accurate to say that a Chief of Staff can been exercising Rukovodjenje in a very real sense but without exercising command. In a short way, is that an accurate statement?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on duties, tasks, that staff of any command is faced with, or rather the Chief of Staff is faced with. It is precisely those duties and tasks that the staff of the Chief of Staff carry out are for the most part dependent on control activities, on the control function, because whatever is done is done in terms of organisation, preparation the drafting of final documents and so on and so forth, with regard to any specific task. And then you move on to the actual implementation, that is to say command. Implementing the work of the staff as personified by the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. I understand. Thank you. Now, there is -- now, just excuse me one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours I'm now going to ask the witness to read into the transcript a short six-line, seven -- six-and-a-half-line passage. This has not previously been translated but I have to say that just today, we've made a decision to use it. So we've provided the translation booth with a photocopy of the Bosnian and I'm just going to ask -- we did this with -- with Mr. Cikotic. It's not ideal, I understand that, but because of the hurry factor we just think we better do it and accomplish what we can. That's what's about to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now -- sorry, Mr. Karavelic, would you please look two paragraphs further down at a section -- at a line beginning "calan," [phoen] I think, "calan 1, 2, 3." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud slowly or just reasonably slowly to help the interpreter that section for seven lines down, up to the section that says "samo jedno lice" [phoen]? So six and a half lines' worth, and if you -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 123 of the constitution of the SFRY singles out the control function. "The president of the Presidency of the SFRY on behalf of the Presidency of SFRY carries out the command of the armed forces of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, in line with this constitution and the federal law." This means that the control function is placed -- the command function, sorry, is placed within the area of competence of the president of the Presidency of SFRY whilst the control function in its entirety, the control of the armed forces, that is, has remained within the area of competence of the Presidency of SFRY. The Presidency is a collegial body for the control of the armed forces, whilst the command function requires one person only.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I just inquire what -- what -- I'm just a bit confused what was being read out. Was that from the previous exhibit? Perhaps that could be put on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes, that should be put on the record. I apologise for that. Yes, it is. It's from the same page of the previous exhibit and it's 3 paragraphs down from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you mind just briefly commenting on what the significance of that passage is that you've read to the Court?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The significance is that everything I've said so far is basically the same as what I've just read out, which means I mentioned that the command function is within the framework of the control function. This has been confirmed by the previous quote, and this quote says, and this is something else that I've mentioned before, that is to say that the staff and the command in its entirety depend on control. And that is confirmed by this quote, and that the entire staff or rather the entire command depends on one person, the commander, that is. And that is stated in the last bit of this quote. That is to say, the command function requires one person only.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. I'm grateful for that. Now, would you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown now the same exhibit but two pages further on? I think it's page 4 of the exhibit, the DD number is DD002758.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, at the bottom of that page is to be found another passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that passage begins with "komandovanje vojnom dzididikom," [phoen] and some of there was read to the witness Cikotic in the past and that was done at page 76 of the transcript of 23rd of February, lines 9 to 11. But, however, on advice now from -- from within our team, there is a slightly longer passage that I want to ask the -- the witness read in and that's what I'm going to do. This also has been provided to the booth so at the bottom of page 176 of the document, page 4 of the uploaded one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Karavelic, do you see the passage that I mentioned there? It's perhaps ten lines from the bottom commencing with the word "komandovanje." [phoen] Do you see that passage?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see two paragraphs starting by the term "command."

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It will be the lower of the two, ten lines from the bottom of the page. Yes, no, pardon me. I take that back because actually there is three on that page. So that was the problem. Yes, not the very bottom one. The one above that, say ten lines from the bottom. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please read those ten lines relatively slowly so that the interpreters can interpret it?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The command of a military unit is carried out by appointed individuals who are appointed as commanders of units, depending on the size and the significance of the units in question, which is established on the basis of the formation of the said unit. The appointment is carried out on the basis of an order, an appointment order or decree. That means that the right of command is in the hands of the appointed individual at any establishment duty. We have to keep in mind that there are certain differences, such as, A, command is related to specific establishment duties; that is, only some positions within the organisation chart or structure are characterised by the right of command. B, if an individual is appointed to such a duty, that individual acquires the right of command within limits established by the regulations of the organisation, by law, with regard to the establishment position in question. That is to say, if a person is appointed as a unit commander, that person acquires the right to command that unit." The end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm very grateful to you for reading that into the transcript for us. Does that accurately state JNA doctrine and also, as a result, Bosnian army doctrine, at the time of 1993?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my understanding, my general understanding of this, I believe that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much for that. I now wish to have you shown a couple of other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, could the witness please be shown on the screen Exhibit 142? This was a book entitled, "Command and control." Again, parts of this were shown to other witnesses. I believe Mr. Cikotic as well, but this is uploaded and translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could I say while that's being done, frankly, I acknowledge as I have acknowledged before, that proceeding in the way that we are does create potential difficulties for the Prosecutor and if there is some way they are caught out or it proves something has gone wrong then the Defence won't, I would think, seek -- seek to oppose any remedy that seems appropriate. I understand it's not -- it's not desirable but I also understand that we don't want to be here on Monday or next week so that's why we've done what we've done. Now, if the witness can be shown, please ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, first of all, just looking at the front page there, do you see the front page of a book and do you know that -- that military textbook, "rukovodjenje i komandovenje" [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so but I'm not sure. I'm not 100 per cent sure here either. There are quite a few such books.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, these books are brought courtesy of Mr. Dzambasovic.

We need to go back to page 18 of the actual document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Do you see a heading entitled, "Number 2, command and control"?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. I won't get you to read this into the transcript because we -- we -- we have it here. But there is a passage which in the Bosnian commences -- commences -- it's the last paragraph there, commencing with the words "ovda je nusdo." [phoen] Do you see that passage? "At this point it is necessary to establish a distinction between control and command." Do you see that section?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Would you mind just reading that as quickly or slowly as you want to and then confirming whether or not that accurately reflects JNA military doctrine, and therefore Bosnian military doctrine in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the passage which the witness is reading is in English on page 14, starting at the words, "at this point," and down to the bottom of that page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, does that passage there accurately reflect JNA military doctrine, and therefore, Bosnian military doctrine in, as you understood it, in 1993?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's nothing special, if we compare it to everything we've said before. It simply confirms everything else, everything we've said before with regard to command and control. There is just one bit bothering me here. When it says, "Command carries out on the basis of orders, directives, and instructions," almost as if only senior officers could issue such orders, and not a command bodies, administration bodies, or whatever. And other -- other bodies. It's not just individuals. So I'm a bit puzzled by this particular bit, but everything else, as far as I can understand, is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And perhaps just to clarify that, as a result of something that was said in the past, was there a different word used for a commander at a lower level than a commander at a higher level in the Bosnian language?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In English, all sorts of levels for leader of a military unit are described as commander, but we have a company commander, and a -- the word in Bosnian is "komandir," and everything higher up is commander, "komandant."

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's the distinction I was interested in. Thank you very much for pointing that out. Good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please now be shown the same exhibit, it's pages 33 to 34 in the Bosnian, and it's page 27 and over to page 28, in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, what's coming now is a section headed, "Number 5, principles of command and control." Once again, this may not prove to be any different to anything you've said before but I just ask for your comment in any event. Do you have that passage there in front of you, "principles of command and control"?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see the end of those principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Perhaps -- well --

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it now, the beginning, at the beginning of the principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Excellent. Sorry, just excuse me a moment. We may be looking at something else now, so -- I'm sorry, we have a small problem of coordination and control of our own on our side here, so just forgive me. I'm sorry, I remember this problem happened last time, yes, it's page 25 in Bosnian, in the Bosnian one. My apologies for that. Okay. Do you have that now, number 5, "principles of command and control," including a subheading of "single authority"?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Would you mind just reading to yourself at whatever speed you like that section five, "principles of command and control," and including the part on single authority. And just read that to yourself and at the end I'll just ask you does that accurately reflect JNA doctrine and Bosnian military doctrine as well.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read through it, if that's the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, that's farce I wish to go with it. Does that accurately state JNA military doctrine and therefore Bosnian military doctrine as well?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These principles of command and control, as far as I can see, have been taken over from certain rules, but I would just like to add something, to emphasise the fact that the principles of command and control in the JNA are regulated in the book called "The Strategy of Armed Combat," and this is a document of crucial significance, issued, published, by the Federal Secretariat for National Defence in the former Yugoslavia. It was published in Belgrade, and this was the most significant document that concerns strategic matters, and it sets forth in detail all these principles of armed combat or rather all these principles of command and control. So this is probably been adopted from that book. In my opinion, that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well, thank you very much. Now there is one final passage from this book that I would like you to be shown, and that is the Bosnian page 29, the English is at pages 35, and over the page to 36. This is a short passage. And where we start is at the heading number 6, functions of command and control. And it's the introductory paragraph to a description of the five functions, but I'm just really interested in a comment on the introductory paragraph. Sorry. It's page 29, I'm sorry, of the Bosnian version. I'm sorry, I have caused the Court staff some difficulties with that, but it's page 29 on the Bosnian page at the bottom left.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading this part on planning. I don't know if that is the end of the relevant section.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, it is at the end of the relevant section. I wasn't going to ask you specifically about the planning function. I was just going to ask you about that introductory paragraph there. It may appear to be more of the same, but could I just ask you could confirm whether or not this is -- this accurately states JNA military doctrine and therefore Bosnian military doctrine at the time?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to say. In 1992 and 1993, we worked in accordance with all the rules, in accordance with all the established doctrines that had been taken over in a -- from the JNA. We followed these rules blindly. Afterwards, and especially after the war, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina gradually tried to transform the doctrine of the eastern bloc into a NATO doctrine. This would be my general point of view. As to whether this was fully carried out, it's hard to say. But on the whole, it was. Although there were certain deviations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. May I just say thank you very much for bearing with those questions? And now I just seek to move to another topic, and that is, when appointing a commander -- now we've been through some of these doctrines in the abstract now, but now I want to come to the concrete case of appointing a commander?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Exhibit 144?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, here we have an order, this is an unrelated to this case but I'm putting it to you as an example of how one can appoint a commander and I just ask for your comments about it. There is a document that's already been tendered. We will just wait for it to come up on the screen. Now, this is a decision and then on the other page there is some more material. Would you mind just having a look at this -- this decision firstly, please, and when you're finished looking at that we'll just look at the other page. You will notice first of all this is from a time that's got little to do with our case. It's from the 20th of August 1992. So I'm just using it to illustrate certain points about appointments and I'll ask for your comments about them. Now, first of all, do you notice that there is a temporary command called JUG [phoen] being set up in a particular or general sector, actually of Igman?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And although you hadn't been appointed at that time, had you, to the position of deputy commander of the 1st Corps, but are you familiar in broad terms with the existence of that group called JUG?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. So what you have in setting up the group JUG on Igman is a specific order establishing that group. Now, do you have the second page now in front of you, the page where the temporary command is established?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay, okay. I'll go -- I'll go through what -- what -- what there is on that page in just a moment, but is this an example of something you described earlier on where you have effectively two parts to an order establishing a temporary command, that the part that establishes that command and then the part that establishes its personnel? Is this what we were talking about before, or an example of what we were talking about before?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think so. Under A, there is a reference to the temporary command of the group JUG south, and we have a list of 11 officers here, and if you have a look at the list, each officer has a different profile, a different professional profile. When I testified about the command of operative groups, I said that depending on the tasks concerned, various sort of individuals, various sort of officers who had various specialties would become part of that group. The group would include officers who specialised in certain fields which were of relevance for the task that had been assigned to the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. And here, the commander is specifically named, and we are moving now to the specific case here, the commander is specifically name that's Dzemal Nejetovic. His chief of staff is specifically named Asim Dzambasovic, and so on. Could you explain to the Tribunal why -- why it's necessary to name those people on an order, and what the importance is of naming those people on an order, and their functions in that way?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a general principle, a general rule in the military. The first and last name of each man must be put down on paper, as well as his duties, his position, in light of which the individual concerned has to carry out certain tasks. For example, under number 4, it says Saric Edib [phoen] will be appointed as chief of security. And as a result of being appointed to this post, this individual has a certain task he has to carry out because there are other rules that state what a certain officer has to do within that service. If the individual has that post on a permanent bases or, for example, on a temporary basis. This is why one proceeds in this manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And just turning from this document to the case of Neretva, the Operation Neretva, you have never been aware of any such document as this in connection with Operation Neretva, in other words, one which sets out who the commander is, who the Chief of Staff is, and who the various branches, officers in charge of those various branches are; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. All right. Thank you, Your Honours. Sorry, excuse me one moment. Sorry, pardon me, I've just been reminded to ask you to note who it is that signed that -- that second page and why is it that Alija Izetbegovic had to sign that second page? Well, in fact, I'll ask you why. Why did Alija Izetbegovic have to sign on the bottom right and what's the function of Sefer Halilovic's signature on the bottom left on that document?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president, Alija Izetbegovic, was the president of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and at the same time the Supreme Commander of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He is the person who would order that such formations at this level be established. I have said this on a number of occasions in the course of my testimony. The establishment of brigades and units at other levels, establishment of commands and units at other levels were his responsibility as well as the -- when it came to appointing commanders or officers at those levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I acknowledge that -- sorry, you go on.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that this document had to have the signature of the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command, but I assume that this document is at the same time a proposal from the chief of the Supreme Command, and there is the signature of the Supreme Commander, as this is a decision, an order, but nothing of any significance has been changed by virtue of this fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Well, yes, I understand that. And now I'm grateful for that explanation. The next topic I want to move to is how one -- perhaps I've just got another question arising from that. But I'll ask it later. Could we move to the issue of the creation of IKMs, now, please I've just got a question about the creation of IKMs. I want to illustrate it by one that seems to be a 1st Corps IKM. Could the witness please be shown Defence document 65 ter number D219? Its court number is DD001107. There is a short -- relatively short order but could a copy please be given to the Prosecutors, as it is more than one page long?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: What's coming up on the screen here, we hope, is a -- an IKM that -- I'll just ask you. Are you aware of this document and is it an IKM created in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be MFI 407.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Perhaps if the witness could be given a chance to look at the back page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document seems familiar to me. It seems to be my document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well, well, I just want to ask you some questions, perhaps could I offer it for tender? Then I'm going to ask some questions about it to establish the structures of an IKM and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I have some questions concerning with the number of this document. It's number 219?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The 65 ter number is 219. That's the handwritten number at the top of the page that Your Honour can see. That's 219. It's MFI 407.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It's admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D407.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, with respect to this document, is it the fact that this document is an order of yours establishing that "particular officers shall constitute the IKM of the 1st Corps at Mount Igman," those officers including as their leader or as their commander I'm sorry, Nedzad Ajnadjic and his deputy Salko Muminovic?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And did you establish, too, various other officers who had to operate different organs of command at that IKM?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And that IKM had under its -- or had to deal with and coordinate and exercise control over the 4th Mechanised Brigade and other units. Were the other units smaller units or were they other brigades as well under that IKM?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was the 4th Hrasnica Brigade a motorised brigade which was within that IKM, and then there was a newly established or the newly established 81st Bosniak Brigade on Igman, which consisted of two Foca brigades that had fallen apart after the problems in July on Igman. And then under the command of that IKM there was also the 9th Mountain Brigade from Tarcin and all these units, all the companies, came from the Sarajevo brigade to hold the defence line in the wider Igman area. And this was under the command of the Igman IKM. There were about, well, almost over 10.000 troops there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That was my next question. It was three brigades and some other units totalling about 10.000 troops and in that IKM you needed --

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 10.000 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And at that point you needed a staff of something in the order of, I think it's accurate to say, just under 20 -- I haven't counted them actually there but I'm -- yes, well, it is 20, 20 staff to run that IKM. Now, in creating that IKM it was very important to you, in order to preserve clarity of command and control and in order to preserve the effectiveness of the IKM to set out quite clearly who was in command, who was the deputy and who had -- which other officers had the various other functions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And it's important to have an order that sets those things out clearly because you don't want temporary functions or -- sorry, temporary units or units governed by an IKM to be subject to any confusion in the chain of command. You want it to be quite clear who has what function and who is able to issue orders to the units in the local area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Once again, with respect to the alleged IKM down in Jablanica early in September or in the middle of September, or indeed at any time in September of 1993, did you ever see any order like this, creating an IKM and -- and enumerating the functions of the staff who were to go there and to perform particular tasks?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having seen anything like this, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. I'm grateful for that. Now, before the break, I'm grateful to you for -- before the break, I was asking you some questions concerning the sending of the troops or -- sorry, the order by Sefer Halilovic directed to you to send -- to provide some troops?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And could the witness now be shown Exhibit P161, which is that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Here we are coming back to Sefer Halilovic's order to you which you obeyed. Okay. You've made yourself very clear about this order and its effect and there are just a couple of details about it -- about this orders and about a couple of other orders which I'm going to show you which I would seek some assistance from you on. Now do you have that order in front of you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. May I just ask you here it's -- in point one, do you -- it says there "prepare the Delta Brigades, parts of the 9th and 10th Mountain Brigades and Solakovic's units totalling some 300 soldiers," and it gives some other details. Now, in terms of the selection of the individual troops, once again, that order did not force you to have any role at all in choosing which particular young men went down to Herzegovina. In other words, the choice of the individual troops. Is that an accurate way of analysing that order? It doesn't place that obligation upon you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what relation you're establishing between the document and the duty or lack of such an obligation for the corps commander to select troops. The document is not about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, yes. Even in my question was silly, you've answered it. Because what I'm really seeking is that the question I've -- the selection of the individual troops to go down to Herzegovina was to be determined at a lower level, by the organs of the 9th and 10th Brigades themselves and Solakovic's units itself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it works, after the order I issued an order to these units of mine. To be more precise to the brigade commands or brigade commanders. And I did this in the same way, in a way similar to the way in which I received the order from General Halilovic. A unit was to be designated or formed, a new unit was to be formed, of a certain strength and it was to be prepared to carry out its tasks. When the brigade commanders received this, no one was preventing them from participating in the selection of the troops, but this was not their obligation. They would forward the case to the level of the battalion, and they would say, I'm going to designate my 2nd Battalion for this task. They will single out 50 or 100 men for me, if possible. If they can single out an establishment company they will do so, if not and quite frequently this was not possible. I have testified about this. Then the battalion commander says, single out a platoon, from a company, and form another company as a temporary unit, which will carry out the task. Once the task has been carried out then all the troops are sent back to their original units, the units that they left in order to form this temporary formation. So it's the command battalion that is the highest level that decides about such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that explanation. And once you issued those orders, you didn't have any part in appointing some sort of a commander over the collection of soldiers which was gathered from your brigade and sent -- sent down to Herzegovina. For example, you didn't select somebody from the 10th Brigade to be in charge of all of these people, did you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. That was within the competencies of the brigade commander and lower levels, battalion level and so on, depending on the size of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, and just to be very clear about that, you did not -- did you know a man called Senad Pecar at that time, from the 10th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I met him. I don't know whether at that very moment I knew him very well or not. That's debatable. However, I do know who Senad Pecar is. It is possible that I had only met him by that time. I think that I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: But certainly you didn't take is Senad Pecar and set him in some position of authority over these three units who went down to Herzegovina; is that correct? In other words, you didn't -- you didn't personally appoint Senad Pecar to do anything in relation to these men; is that true?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And in fact it may well be that you hadn't even met Senad Pecar at that time; is that also true?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very likely that I hadn't met him at that time. However, while he was on Igman, it is possible that we had some telephone contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand. The last question -- or there are two other questions I've got about that document. One is the mention of the 6th Corps Command taking over these troops which you can see at the end of the paragraph number 1. Now, in relation to that, were you aware of what role, if any, the 6th Corps Command was going to play with respect to these troops? In other words, did you know whether or not these troops were to be resubordinated to the 6th command or not?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right now, I couldn't tell you. I can only tell you something based on the documents which are pertinent to what you are asking me about. Everything else would depend on how the communications transpired in the field. I don't know. I wouldn't know whether somebody received orders or not, whether the units were supposed to be resubordinated to one command or to the other command. I couldn't tell you that because I don't know. I truly can't be of assistance in this matter, and I don't think that it would be appropriate for me to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, no. Well, I stand --

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People from the field could tell you much more about that, those who were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, thank you for that, and it's really just the orders itself that I'm concentrating on in your case. The second paragraph there, that -- could I just ask that? Is that really something by way of a personal comment passing between you and Mr. Halilovic as a result of discussions you had and as a result of the genuine fears that you had at the time, that taking away your mobile reserve might endanger Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I could agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Because in military terms, would you agree with this? It's a pretty meaningless thing for him to say that he would be prepared to bear full responsibility for the fall of Sarajevo? Would you agree with that comment of mine?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. I take it this it was a time when there was a lot of pressure on all military commanders, you, Sefer Halilovic, Rasim Delic and the whole lot of you, frankly.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Analysing that nowadays, and I could see it even during the war, let alone nowadays, that if Herzegovina and Mostar had fallen, then defending Sarajevo would be pointless. It would just be a matter of time when Sarajevo would fall as well. And this is why it is very important to look at it as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Last question on that topic. The Delta Brigade didn't go. Do you remember what -- what happened to the Delta Brigade? Did they just refuse to talk to you or what occurred with them?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I have partially answered that question already. Namely, I said that the dates are not fully clear to me, the dates when the Delta Brigade came under my command, or became a part of the 1st Corps. I would have to take a look at the documents to refresh my memory. This could be one of the reasons. However, my personal view is that even if this was one of the reasons, it wasn't the only one. Regardless of whether it became a part of the 1st Corps or not, I ought to have issued an order, and I don't know whether the order was indeed issued, and even if it did not become part of the 1st Corps, it should have had and it is most likely that General Halilovic issued that order because he believed that it was already part of the 1st Corps. Now, as to whether it was under my command or not, that's debatable. There were certain problems involved. Whether I was unable to send the unit because the command and the commander of the brigade were dissatisfied on a number of issues, that is possible. In a way, they sometimes felt that they were a unit of the Supreme Command, and then they were a unit of the Supreme Command Staff, and were supposed to be relegated to the level of the corps which they thought was a kind of a humiliation. I don't know if that's the right word. And there were many other reasons. There was a lot of disobedience and lack of respect for the chain of command. So it is possible that there are many reasons for the fact that that unit was not sent out. However, I would need to get in touch with certain people and take a look at some documents in order to give you a full and accurate answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm grateful to you for what you've given there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness now please be shown -- just excuse me, I'm sorry. Thanks, yes, pardon me, finally, there is just one other point about that. Well, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: On the face of that document there, I understand you don't know the -- the realities of what happened down in the Neretva valley but on the face of that document, does it appear to you that the -- I withdraw that question. I'll withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'd now like the witness, please, to be shown Exhibit P -- Exhibit 290, 290.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Karavelic, what's now happening I'm now moving through those days at the time when Sefer Halilovic sent the order and you then complied with that order and gave some orders yourself. I'm not going to take you to those orders that you gave. You've already talked about those with the -- with the Prosecutors. But I now want to move to the -- the 5th of September, when a note came from you down to Sefer Halilovic personally and you sent it to him at Jablanica, Jablanica. Do you have that in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, it may be that you can't remember the details of sending a handful -- not a handful, but a couple of hundred troops out of the district. But I just want to see whether you can remember any details about a particular part of this. If you can, you can. If you can't, you can't. But would you just look at this section here where it says, four lines or so down, it says "at 2230 hours, when the motor vehicles arrived, Caco and Celo personally proposed to me that the departure be postponed for 24 hours," and then the next sentence reads like this: "However, after that in the course of the day today it was put off completely." Now, I'm going to ask you what you remember about each of those steps along the way. Do you recall, yourself, that discussion when Caco and Celo personally proposed to you to put off the departure for 24 hours? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one point in time, I touched upon this in one of my answers. I don't remember exactly whether it was me personally who talked to Caco and Celo, or whether that was done by my assistants, my deputy, my Chief of Staff, because they had numerous contacts, they had to be in touch with the units continuously. So they were continuously in telephone and other contact with them. So it's possible that will they prepared this. It is possible that they talked to Caco and Celo. However, it is also possible that I talked to them. I couldn't tell you how it was. I remember that there were some problems with the time schedule at the time, and deadlines. Now, whether they tried to avoid that or not, I really couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Therefore, in my own terms, there was a lot of hesitation and clashes there. There were constant -- there was constant pressure applied, constant requests, and continuous problems of all kinds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, and even though you can't remember all the details, which we understand, this just looks like another example of these two units not being in the proper line of control and command, because Halilovic had ordered you to -- to provide troops, and you'd ordered them to provide troops, but now we have that it was put off completely. Do you agree with that, that this was just another one of those failures in the line of command and control?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by the circumstances, yes. This all fits in. Now, in relation to your question whether it is 100 per cent consistent or less, I couldn't tell you. However, there is some truth in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And I understand, too. Yes, I understand that. But clearly, Halilovic gave you an order, you gave these men an order, and then these men did not carry out that order. And so much is apparent on the face of this document, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not exactly. If you want me to say that they failed to carry this out and that this is a result of the failure to abide by the chain of command, I couldn't say whether it was that or some objective circumstances, such as bad weather, as a result of which I consciously agreed to postpone it because later on the units indeed departed. From the distance nowadays it would be hard for me to say which of these two prevailed. It is possible that both reasons existed. I'm trying to be as frank as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand that. But just to assist you with that, could we just look at the second page in the English version, please? I'm sorry, Mr. Karavelic, I think it's all on one page for you but for us it's broken up. Do you see the second -- do you see the paragraph, paragraph 2, saying "the vehicles that you sent are located at Hrasnica and there are no problems with them, let us know how you -- how to proceed with these vehicles." Let me just ask you this: It may sound speculative and if it is you can tell us that you can't answer it, but it's -- it's not likely that you would have countermanded the order for those units to go to Herzegovina without telling Sefer Halilovic or the inspection team that you'd countermanded that order. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You put several questions. I don't know whether I should answer with a yes or a no. I'm not sure, just to be clear on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'll try again. If -- you raised a couple of possibilities as to why it was that these troops didn't go down to Herzegovina a minute ago, and I just wanted today's ask you this: If it was a decision by you that they shouldn't have gone, then in accordance with the proper approach, you would have let Sefer Halilovic know and you would have let -- I'll keep it to Sefer Halilovic. You would have let Sefer know, "Look, I'm not sending those troops for the following reason." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly, yes, that's how it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. So given the information on this document, whilst you can't remember exactly what happened, would you agree it's likely that this was some form of failure to comply with the chain of control and command which led to the units not departing whether they should, even though they did depart later on; do you agree with that proposition?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said. I think I've fully answered the question you put just now in my previous answer to your previous question. I do not exclude the possibility, but I cannot confirm to what extent each of the reason was responsible. If Ramiz Delalic, Celo, would come here to testify he would be the best person to say that. Unlike Caco who is unable to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: We'll ask him. Thank you, Mr. Karavelic. Very well. I'm sorry, Your Honours, could I just inquire now what time urns are proposing I'm going to move on to another topic now and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Could you please tell me first how long are you going to need?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, as history has shown, if I just have a moment to gather my thoughts I think the witness and counsel and perhaps the Judges as well get tired as time goes by. I'm still very hopeful to finish today, and I'm going to press on to do that. I would rather appreciate having a short break if that were possible now, just to collect my thoughts. There are a very finite number of topics left to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we could have the break right now, and we will resume at 20 minutes past 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey? You have something to inform us?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have. I've been considering the issue of finishing tonight and I believe that it can be done. But in looking at the -- at the amount of time spent, I think the Prosecution have had more than double the time that the Defence have with this particular witness. Now, the way I think it can be done is this. I -- there was a number of transcripts I wanted to question him about. What I proposed in the past was to talk to the Prosecutors about these transcripts and see if we could find any middle ground about it and we agreed to talk but we have been too busy to actually do that. Therefore I propose to leave those out. With the witness Salko Gusic that -- you'll recall there was a time limit like this imposed, and what we decided was that if needs be the witness might be able to give some limited extra evidence later by videolink to which, of course, the Defence would agree if the Prosecution would. In the event that we couldn't resolve the matters that we needed to resolve otherwise. In that way, I think I can complete it tonight. That's what I propose to do. If I feel that we have been shut out from dealing with a couple of relevant issues, I might ask that the witness be recalled at a later time. However, I think it's rational to expect that we can resolve those problems. That's my belief. I think we -- there's a couple that the Prosecution might want and that we might. So for those reasons and given that, if I'm able to -- to ignite the recalling mechanism, if I need to, at a future stage by videolink, then I would be comfortable to say we'll finish tonight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your information. As for the videolink issues, I believe that you have to file something in written to the attention of this Bench at a later stage because now it's very difficult to predict how far we could go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honours, and I won't take more time talking about it. We are in a difficult position here. In reality, I could go on for significantly more time but we are living in the real world so I'll now continue to ask the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As for the -- yes, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The transcripts, I'm not sure what my learned friend is talking about, there being some agreement about some transcripts he wanted to cross-examine on. Could he enlighten us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe just like we have we have at our hands for this transcript, maybe Mr. Morrissey will ask some questions concerning the testimonies of other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, that was part of it. But -- sorry. But there is also some telephone intercept material which the Prosecution has and there is obviously some that we have and we need to discuss on what basis that can be admitted. It would take an argument to be had. Now, we don't have time for it so, frankly, that's why I say I would rather put that off. If the Prosecutors and we can agree on terms of admissibility for such things then there won't be any need for any arguments about it. That's what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, well, that may be a subject for the proposed status conference if there is any -- as for that, I believe that the Defence should draft the topics they would like to talk about and next Monday, I hope the parties will sit together to go over those issues one by one to see how far you could go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: If there is still any problems pending on next Tuesday, the Defence should inform the Bench and we will see whether we could hold a kind of Status Conference next week, sometime next week. I'm not sure. Of course, saying this, we will bear in mind there is an objection from the Prosecution on this issue. Yes. Could we have the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown D146.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: We are now returning to the order of the 30th of August, for another five to ten minute period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could that document please be shown to the witness? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Do you have that document in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I just want to ask you some questions about certain components in this order which may bear upon the question of the interpretation of the word "rukovodjenje" in this order. I'm going to put them to you one by one and I'll ask you to comment on them as you see fit. First of all, could I just ask you to note that when you look at this order here, that in point 3, a specific power to issue orders is given to the Chief of Staff of the SVK. Do you see that specific power given there in point 3, a power to solve problems in the field by issuing orders?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. When considering the ambit of the word "rukovodjenje" up in paragraph number 1, is it a relevant fact that the drafter of this document felt the need to give a specific command power to the Chief of Staff thus possibly implying a limit on the ambit of the term "rukovodjenje" in paragraph 1? Do you have a comment on that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we keep item 3 on the screen? Item 3 provides the answer to your question, where it says "to solve problems through his orders, and inform me regularly of it, and in case of radical proposals and solutions, it is necessary to consult me," which indicates what the limits are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And in terms of interpreting that term "rukovodjenje" which is up in paragraph number 1, if that word "rukovodjenje" was to be given its full meaning as including a power to command, then paragraph 3 would be entirely unnecessary. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's hard for me to say, and be sure 100 per cent that this is how it is because these are general issues, issues of principle, and this is -- this is why the sentence where it says that Rasim Delic does not allow Sefer Halilovic to do anything radical through his orders without consulting him. Now, what does the term "radical" entail? We don't know. Only Rasim Delic could reply to that, or, rather, Sefer Halilovic as well. He can also provide his opinion as to why Rasim Delic formulated this ban on him not being able to do something without consulting Rasim Delic, which means that Rasim Delic is behind all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just in the bottom left, do you see the initials ADZ/IH? And could I ask you when you look at them does that mean that this document was drafted up for Rasim Delic by Asim Dzambasovic and another person?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, that's quite likely, if not certain, unless there is someone else who has the initials A.DZ., because at the time he had already left me in the command of the 1st Corps while he was the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. What I'm doing here, I understand, I'm just asking you for comments as you go along. I've put that particular one to you. There is another one I want to put to you and ask you what effect that has on the interpretation of the term "rukovodjenje," and that is the preamble of this document altogether. Do you see that the preamble hear reads and could the witness be given the chance to look at the preamble on the screen, the preamble provides that "in accordance with -- effectively with the Zenica meeting, and with the aim of eliminating current shortcomings and weaknesses in the zones of responsibility of the 4th and 6th Corps the order is passed." In other words, the purpose being to follow through with what happened at Zenica and to fix up the 4th and 6th Corps, is the preamble there something that an officer would look at when trying to work out what the extent of the meaning -- what the extent of the powers under that order are? In other words, is the preamble something relevant to interpreting the rest of the document? I think that's probably the best way to put it.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually, there is always a preamble. I don't know how this is translated in English but the part preceding the word, "I order" is the part that we call a preamble, and in that preamble one usually briefly states the purpose of the order, or, rather, the reason for which the order is being drafted, or rather, the reason for which what follows below is set forth. In this preamble, it mentions a meeting held in Zenica on the 21st of August. So it's quite logical to expect that each and every officer would have a look at the conclusions from the meeting and he would draw the conclusion that one should bear in mind the conclusions from that meeting and the zone of responsibility of the 4th and 6th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. There are two other matters I wanted to raise. The first one is having regard to the reference to the zones of responsibilities of the 4th and 6th Corps, is it accurate to say that whatever powers there are in this order have got nothing to do with units of the 3rd Corps, so far as you can see?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the case in my opinion, too, because it's quite explicitly stated that it concerns the zone of responsibility of the 4th and 6th Corps here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Finally could we look at the 4th point there, on that list, which indicates that the monitoring should begin on the 31st of August and be completed by an unspecified date, and then it's required that a written report be written on return. Now let me just ask you about that. Is it the fact that an inspection team's mission is completed when it reports, unless of course it's extended by some other order?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to be clear as to how one usually proceeded. Item 4 says "when one should commence," but it doesn't say when it should be ended. Perhaps for other reasons, I don't want to guess what reasons. Perhaps there was an agreement between the commander of the Supreme Command and the Chief of Staff because it was impossible to know when this could be ended. So in the second paragraph, under item 4, it says upon completion when you're ready to submit a written report, then the inspection should come to an end, in accordance with this order. There were such cases, but everything depends on the contact that the commander of the Supreme Command and the Chief of Staff had. Everything depends on what they had agreed on orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that. Are you aware that the inspection team in fact reported on the 20th of September upon return from Herzegovina up to Sarajevo? Are you aware of that as a fact or not?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I heard about that recently but I don't believe that I saw that document. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's okay. At all events, am I right -- well, is this proposition correct, that whenever -- whenever the inspection team did report, then, unless there was another order in place, that report signals the end of the inspection team? Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult for me to answer your question by saying yes or no, because the written document could always be changed because of a verbal agreement. This is how it should have been, but it does not necessarily mean that this is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. We may be agreeing entirely over this. What I'm putting to you is that if there was another order that could have changed things, but if there was no other order, then this inspection team finished when the inspection report was produced. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how things should have been, more or less. Because even when there was drafted, one could say that's one of the reports continue with your work. Or perhaps that wouldn't be said. This is something that one could discuss at far greater length.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, thank you very much for those explanations. Now, could we move please now -- just one second, please. Sorry, I just want to show the witness -- I'm sorry, just excuse me one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, the document I -- MFI 385, please. Thank you. This is a document that in respect of which questions have been asked about whether it's a genuine document or not, and those are the questions I have to ask you. So could that document please be shown on the screen? And in particular the Bosnian version, could that be shown to everyone?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, with respect to this document, this is a document concerning the sending of the 2nd independent -- on its face it's a document sending the 2nd Independent Battalion down to Herzegovina. Now, I wanted to ask you a question about this. First of all, do you have that on your screen?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
