utterances.text: Now, there is no suggestion that -- there is no critical questions of you about this but I just have to -- have to test it. Your signature on that document there, is that a handwritten signature or a signature, a pre-made, rubberised stamp?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you move the document so I can have a look at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I wonder if the witness could be shown a closeup of that particular part? If it could be zoomed in on the stamp and on the signature? I'm sorry, I believe there is a technical problem. I can continue to ask some questions, anyway, so as not to waste time while that's being fixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You indicated in examining that document -- when you were asked questions about that, you thought it was possible that there was a number 2 contained within that 1st Corps stamp. Do you see that now?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the stamp? I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry I've jumped from the signature to the stamp, yes. Very well. Well, first of all, is that stamp a -- a proforma rubber stamp or is it a natural bit of handwriting by you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to my signature in the form of a stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm referring to the cursive script writing there. Was that -- is that a handwritten signature. Sometimes people have a signature that's pre-made and that's I'm asking you, if that's what it is or not.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This signature has nothing to do with a stamp, nor does the stamp have anything to do with the signature. These two things are quite separate from each other. They were never linked, if that's your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's okay. And so the signature there was a signature done by your hand, is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one could ask oneself whether this is a signature, my own signature, whether this is something that I signed, or whether it was a facsimile of my signature, a facsimile of my signature or, rather, a stamp because I signed in this way. But my facsimile was like this too. But I very rarely gave my facsimile signature to others. That would happen very rarely, almost never, so it is really of no great importance whether it is an original signature or not is really not of much importance because I always had it on me. I had it in my wallet. I had my facsimile signature in my wallet. I never really gave it to anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. You indicated when being questioned by my learned friend the Prosecutor that you thought you'd seen a number 2 or it was possible that there was a number 2 within that stamp. Do you see any such number 2 there?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly didn't say that I saw the number 2, if we are talking about the stamp now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, we are, and it must have been my mistake about that, I'm sorry. Could you clarify whether or not you did say such a thing?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. We can see a stamp here. It says 1. Corps, the 1st Corps, and there is the coat of arms of Bosnia-Herzegovina and at the time I said the corps had two kinds of stamps. And because of the existence of an IKM, because it was necessary for an IKM to operate, and we mentioned an order of mine a while ago about forming an IKM. As far as I can remember, on one of the stamps below the coat of arms, there was the number 2, and such stamps do exist. I don't know whether that means that on the basic stamp, the one that didn't come from the corps command, I don't know whether that means that this basic stamp should contain the number 1 or whether it was taken for granted that if stamp -- the stamp that contained the number 2 meant that the other one should refer to number 1. I can't be certain about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay, now you've clarified that issue and thank you. Just one other question about that order, sending the 2nd Independent Battalion away. A number of troops indicated -- I can't give names, unfortunately, but a number of people who have indicated that when they left they were told that they were going to be resubordinated to Zuka, that they were going to go to the -- Zuka's base at Donja Jablanica and they were going to be resubordinated to Zuka. Now, that's the evidence we have to deal with in this Court and I just want your comment on that. Do you recall saying that to any of the troops when they set off, from your own memory now?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said that they said that they were going to be resubordinated to Zuka. I don't know that is something that they were told. As far as I can remember in the brief, addressed this unit from the company, from the 9th Motorised. I didn't address any other units. I didn't say anything like that. I didn't know that they were subordinated to Zuka until I saw that order. Quite by chance I saw a copy of that order, perhaps two years ago when I signed the third statement in Sarajevo. I wasn't aware of it up until that time, and I really couldn't have told them anything of this sort in Sarajevo in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. Thank you for those answers. I wants to move on now to the order of commander -- sorry, the instruction that purports to come from Commander Delic on the 12th of September. It's Exhibit 157. Now, this document is one that you've already looked at. The Prosecutor showed you. This is a document which is under the name of Rasim Delic, and I've got some questions for you about -- about it, to investigate whether it's genuine or not, and first of all, I -- do you have that in front of you now on the screen?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, the first thing is, in the preamble there, sorry, I won't trouble you with the preamble now. With respect to paragraph number 2, you'll notice there that there is a reference to a genocide, an apparent -- that's what the document says, "the genocide committed against the civilian population by members of the 1st Corps, 9 Mountain Brigade." Now, at around this time, and I mean, you know, around the 11th, 12th, and 13th of September, at approximately the time when you got that coded report from the 2nd Independent Battalion, Rasim Delic did not call you and ask you whether you knew anything about this supposed genocide, did he? In fact, you heard nothing about it through official channels; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: So although there is some -- there is talk in this document that a unit from the 1st Corps has committed things, has committed genocide, in fact -- well, sorry, I'm making a comment, I won't make it. I'll withdraw that. Go now to the last sentence in that paragraph where it says, "Order the 1st Corps, 9th Brigade deputy commander to return to Sarajevo immediately in order to solve problems in the unit." Now, that document appears to say nothing about returning any units to Sarajevo but rather talks about returning the deputy commander to Sarajevo. What I want to ask you is: Did you personally request Commander Delic to send Ramiz Delalic, Celo, back to Sarajevo to solve, and I quote, "problems in the unit"?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Did you ask Commander Delic -- I have to say we are not blaming Commander Delic for this. We were asking whether this order is genuine at all --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object to that. I mean, how can the witness possibly answer whether the document is genuine, if the order is genuine? He's never seen it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that's the purpose of the cross-examination, but actually, I don't think Mr. Morrissey will ask this question to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'll just ask him about what he did in order to build up that one part of our picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Any way, you've already answered one question about it and I'll ask you another one. Did you ask Rasim Delic to send anyone back from -- from Herzegovina, whether it be Ramiz Delalic or any other person? At that time, I should make clear.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't think so. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Very well, those are the questions about that particular order. Now, thank you. I'm sorry, I'm just keeping an eye on the time here, Mr. Karavelic. Very well. Now, on or about the 20th of September, were you aware that Sefer Halilovic and Rifat Bilajac and the team, the inspection team, all came back to Sarajevo at approximately the same time that your units were returned to you and returned to your line of control and command? That question has become a monster and I'll start it again. Did you become aware that Sefer and the inspection team had come back at around the 20th of September?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's really difficult for me to confirm such a date. I had problems of my own. I had my daily duties to perform. And I did not have the right to monitor what my superior was doing. I think that General Halilovic did come to Sarajevo, I don't know why. I really don't know and I wouldn't want to speculate and answer your question erroneously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's okay. I could ask you another question which might help. Did Sefer Halilovic come back to Sarajevo at approximately the same time 14 that your units did? That the units you'd sent out came back to your command and control?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when the unit from the 9th and 10th returned, let alone when Sefer Halilovic returned. I really couldn't answer your question precisely, because I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you've indicated, you've given the evidence that you want to give about the order that you received to find some more troops to send back to -- back to Herzegovina. I just want to show you some later documents that may be relevant to that. Oh, perhaps there is one other thing. After Sefer Halilovic and the inspection team came back, were you aware of whether the rest of the team, Karic, Zulic, Bilajac, ever went back down to Herzegovina or not? Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't say anything about that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'd like the witness now to be shown Exhibit 132 following which we'll show Exhibit 133.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: These -- you're about to be shown some letters now which may or may not have been -- you may or may not have seen yourself but they have been tendered into evidence here and I just want your comment here about them. So Exhibit 132 is a letter from Sefer Halilovic to Rasim Delic, and I don't need to be -- you don't need to be concerned about the -- the references to Pasalic. It's really the issue about Salko Gusic that I want to you comment on. Now, here, you'll see at the second prong, the following passage: "Although with your permission I said to Salko Gusic the commander the 6th Corps that we would see each other at Jablanica on Saturday, he has not shown up yet or contacted me. This has become his habit." And then Halilovic goes on to say a couple more things about that. Then he goes on to observe this: "He seems to have taken it very seriously that I cannot order him, which is basically what I do not want. However, it would be only fitting if he or someone from the corps command at least contacted me because there is fierce fighting going on here." Now, I'll show you another document from -- from Commander Delic in a minute but to your understanding, does that passage there suggest to you that Sefer Halilovic was in a position to issue commands to Salko Gusic at the time of that letter?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In legal terms, one may wonder whether he had the right to issue orders to Salko Gusic. As to how it was in practise, I couldn't say because I don't know what sort of terms Sefer Halilovic and General Delic were on. I don't know what sort of contact they had. I don't know what sort of relation they had, what sort of a relationship they had. From this paragraph you can quite clearly see that the command of the 6th Corps -- I wouldn't want to use an ugly term -- he was trying to extricate himself from a situation perhaps. I don't know why. Perhaps he was trying to avoid Sefer Halilovic. These are very delicate issues. It's difficult for me to comment on them because I really wasn't involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand. Very well. I just ask for your comment to the extent you can, and I understand what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could we move on to the next document, please, that is Exhibit 133? Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Do you now see -- this is an order from Rasim Delic, both to Sefer Halilovic personally and to the 6th Corps commander personally which gives certain orders and instructions to them?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, what I want you to comment on here is -- is this issue. In this document, Sefer Halilovic is addressed as the chief of the SVK, in other words in his capacity as Chief of Staff. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it says, in the first item of the order. And also in the heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And in paragraph number 2, it's apparent that at this point, the chief of the -- Chief of Staff, Sefer Halilovic, has prepared, has planned and prepared, or as formed an idea or plan concerning combat operations to begin in that area. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here clearly, it is hereby ordered to the commander of the 6th Corps to locate the chief of the Supreme Command Staff, to report to him, and to commence with planning and preparation of combat activities. This probably refers to the commander of the 6th Corps, because naturally, the Supreme Command Staff and its chief, who represents the staff, are the one who is are most familiar with the general idea, which is completely logical in military terms. This is simply the idea, the general idea, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the comment in the previous letter by Halilovic that -- that Gusic regarded him as unable to command him and that Halilovic did not purport to want to command him, do you agree that it appears here that Halilovic is performing with respect to these proposed combat operations, a staff sort of coordinating type of function whereas the direct line of command goes from Delic, Commander Delic, down to Salko Gusic? Is that how it appears to you based on the two documents you've seen?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question is fully clear to me. And this is what I would say to that question. What you're trying to get me to answer in response to your question is not something that is completely unknown. There were, indeed, elements of that within the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, whether that was the case here and if so, to what extent, in this particular case, that is something that is very difficult for me to say, because all communications went above me and beyond me. Therefore, it is very -- also difficult for me to say in response to that document where Jovo Divjak wrote something as a deputy of the Chief of Staff about him being isolated from certain activities and so on, so any response that I might give to that would, to a certain extent, be improper because I cannot tell you what was the relationship between Rasim Delic and Jovo Divjak. It is very difficult to judge that. So I hope that you will be satisfied with my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand and I will move on from that. I want to go now to the issue of -- of the operation of Trebevic. Now, turning to Trebevic, because you -- you took an important part in the, if I may say, direct military side of Operation Trebevic in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: We've heard evidence from General Jasarevic in this court already and it's fair to state that he also and his service played a significant role in planning and carrying out that operation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Would --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Exhibit 261, D261?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: What's about to be shown to you now is a document -- it's an action plan I think for Operation Trebevic which has your name and a number of other people upon it and I just want to show it to you and you can confirm what it is, if you're prepared to. While that's being brought up, could I just ask you this question? Did you become aware, in the course of preparing Operation Trebevic, that the SVB services would take this opportunity to investigate more fully a number of crimes that were outstanding to be investigated, including the crime at Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear about that, nor did I know about that all the way up until the Trebevic plan. I also didn't know about that in the course of implementation of the Trebevic plan. That's how it was, as far as I am concerned. However, soon after the Trebevic plan, such stories started circulating.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I can just ask you this: It wasn't necessary -- it wasn't required of the SVB to inform you about their criminal investigations one way or the other; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that they did not have that duty, and even if they did have it, they wouldn't have done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: After the operation, Trebevic, had succeeded in a military sense, did you become aware, while you were carrying out your other military duties that the SVB was in fact interviewing numerous arrested people from the two brigades?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that because a large number of my staff participated in taking 2 to 300 people to prison upon completion of the Trebevic plan, and all of them were questioned and so on, and I have not learned anything about the results of such investigations to this date. I was never briefed by anyone on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, and I think you've explained to the Prosecutor what the relationship was. But I just want to ask you this question, too. In terms of the SVB's ability to take statements and to interview persons from the 9th Brigade back in Sarajevo, I understand it's not your responsibility but I just want to did you about the realities of doing that. To your knowledge, the 9th Brigade, whilst it might cooperate in combat activities was unlikely to cooperate in criminal investigations. Is that an accurate statement?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, it is very difficult for me to be clear and accurate. I cannot really answer there question because I don't know how to answer. I would need to have much more information in order to be able to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps given your answers about that, I'll just restrict myself to one general, theoretical question about it. From where you -- from where you stood at the time, in a theoretical sense, did it make sense for the SVB, if they had outstanding criminal investigations to do into crimes at Grabovica, to delay interviewing persons, witnesses, or others, until Trebevic was carried out so that the -- so that their investigations could happen in a unit that was brought under the line of command and control? In other words, did it make sense for them to wait?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Analysing it from a military point of view, I, as a military professional, analysing it only in those terms, believe that there was no reason to postpone anything, and to delay it. Now, as to whether that did happen and if so, under whose influence, is something I couldn't tell you because I lack the -- I don't have the necessary information. I know that in that respect, I never obstructed the work of my security service, which was working on this, and had my security service received orders from Jasarevic to do that, it would have done so, or in other terms, had I been ordered to do that I would have done it with my security service. However, I was never instructed to do that, nor did my security service ever seek any instructions or approvals from me, although it is not duty-bound to do that because it needs to take the matters to the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand that, just the last point that you made there is one that I just wanted to clarify. If it turns out that Sacir Arnautovic did in fact endeavour to take statements from 9th Brigade people, he wasn't duty bound to tell you about that investigative process, was he?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it wasn't, but I cannot now claim that I am 100 per cent familiar with the rules and regulations of the security service. I suppose that it wasn't. However, I don't know that he did it because he never told me about that. Therefore, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Final question is that did you become aware, in 1995, or 1996, that Sefer Halilovic called for the perpetrators of the crimes at Grabovica to be investigated and dealt with according to law?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The relevance of that is what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think there is obvious relevance to this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The question is just in broad terms did you become aware of Sefer Halilovic making such a call in 1995 and 1996?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I heard about that. However, I cannot substantiate it, and nobody told me anything officially, nor did I see any documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That puts an end to any questions about that. Thank you for your patience in answering the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, subject to what I said earlier on, that is the end of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any redirect examination? Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There is, only, not very much, but thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Karavelic, yesterday my learned colleague, Mr. Morrissey, asked you about the Geneva Conventions and training of members or soldiers in your corps in relation to the Geneva Conventions. My question is: Was there any formal training system for training the lower-ranking soldiers in their obligations under the Geneva Conventions and in the laws of war?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please clarify your question? What are you referring to when you are mentioning formal training system?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was there a formal system within the corps of educating the lower-ranking or unranked members, soldiers, in the laws of war, the treatment of civilians, the treatment of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You just put a very difficult question, very difficult because this is a huge question, whether there was a training. Naturally, upon hearing your question, I assume that what you mean is whether there were any plans, first at the level of the corps command, going down until the lowest level, the squad and platoon, plans to educate officers, which is quite natural and mandatory in the peacetime army or in the army which is at war but in the circumstances where the entire army is not engaged in a war. For example, that could happen in a case where one of the NATO countries would send their army to Iraq and a unit sent to Iraq would need to have such a training before being deployed there. Or any other unit going from a country elsewhere would need to be trained before being able to accomplish its assignment. Now, in order to apply this system in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I think that the Defence, through their questions, wanted to find out exactly how the brigades were established and how the commanders became commanders, and so on, so I can give you a general reply. But before I give you the reply, I want to say the following. The Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina consisted of ordinary people, young men and old men, all of them, every one of them, were patriots, and there was no selection as to their abilities and intelligence levels. Now to go back to your question, I had an assistant for legal matters within the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could I just --

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to serve justice, I'm prepared to work until midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We can't --

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will be brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We've got to stop at 7. I'm asking you whether there was a system?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will be brief. I had an assistant for legal issues. The assistant for legal issues had to and must have produced such documents and clarified such documents and ensured that these documents reached the lowest-ranking soldiers and that all of them were aware of this. There were plans to educate and to train. Now, here is my answer. Had this training been implemented as it is done in an American unit before it is sent to an assignment, no. It wasn't done. However, there was some training. That is a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who was the training of? Which level was the training carried out? Senior officers? Junior ones?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were -- that was done on all levels, both for senior and junior officers. All of the officers had to be informed and made familiar with basic principles and rules of the international law and Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What percentage of soldiers in the corps, to your understanding, received this training?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the four years of war, I believe that a large percentage of officers were familiarised with that very well, but I cannot guarantee you that 100 per cent of the officers were trained. As for the troops, it would be very difficult for me to estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Today, this is at page 68 of the transcript, in response to a question from my learned colleague, Defence counsel, you said that you didn't see an order appointing Sefer Halilovic as the commander of anything. My question to you is: What was your understanding of who was to command the units that you sent to Herzegovina upon Sefer Halilovic's request in early September 1993?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My reply is as follows: I sent the units to Jablanica upon the order of the Chief of the Supreme Command Staff. By doing so, by sending the units upon the order of the Chief of the Supreme Command Staff, the units were duty bound to report at the place and the Chief of the Supreme Command Staff was just one of the persons deciding what to do with the corps units. And what I said is you don't really expect the Chief of the Supreme Command Staff to command two or three units, companies. This is why these units were resubordinated to somebody else. From a military point of view, this was quite proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: My learned colleague, Mr. Morrissey, also asked you some questions about the map, the Operation Neretva map, which is Exhibit D131. I just want you to have another look at it. Rather than going to the trouble of putting up the original, I'll just show you this one, which is the copy of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I didn't show him the map on any occasion, did I? From recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I didn't say that he did. I said he asked you questions about the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, if the questions were asked. I believe that any --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm happy to see how far it goes, but if -- the questions have to be very much in response to what I asked. It's re-examination, but we'll see where it goes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I do understand the purpose of re-examination. The question that Mr. Morrissey put to you, just to satisfy him that this is re-examination, at page 71, was, quote, "By looking at the map, you can't determine who was in command of combat activities in the Neretva valley in September 1993." Your response was, and I'm paraphrasing to an extent, the map is not a complete document covering all combat activities in full, unquote. My question to you is, following from that, to clarify it, if the map were the only document relating to the combat activities, looking at it, what would it tell you about who was in command of the operation Neretva which is inscribed in the top of it?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now this is what you are asking me, if the map were the only document and nothing else existed, well, the map speaks for itself. I am a soldier. I cannot tell you anything else other than what is stated on the map, and that is the name of the person who produced the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: My question is, what would it tell you about who is in command of the combat marked and the map, inscribed "Operation Neretva," in the absence of any other documents?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through my testimony and everything else, you were able to see just how many times the Defence quoted certain portions of books, regardless of whether these books can be considered formal sources, and you could see how contradictory these quotes were. Now you are putting a question to me invoking my abilities as a professional soldier, and I have to tell you that this is a really hypothetical question, a question that would require me to study this in great depth in order to give you an answer. This is something that an expert should do, and not only upon studying this very thoroughly, the expert still would not be able to simply answer it and say Sefer Halilovic was a commander or was not a commander. The expert would give you an answer that would have a very large number of various elements. I'm trying to clarify it in the following terms. It is clear that this map was produced by Sefer Halilovic. It was approved by Rasim Delic. But these two persons should be viewed as one. Rasim Delic was the commander. Sefer Halilovic was the Chief of Staff. So if we look at the map only, this is how it is. This map doesn't mean that the combat activities were indeed implemented. Now, if you were to ask me something else, if you were to say this map was implemented and combat activities were carried out in accordance with this map, then a large number of other questions would ensue from this as to exactly what happened out there in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What do you mean Rasim Delic and Sefer Halilovic should be viewed as one?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a certain sense, that's quite correct, because the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command and the commander of the Supreme Command have to think in an identical manner, have to draft documents as if they were just one body when it comes to leading the army, when it comes to combat activities. Because at the very beginning, when Defence counsel put certain questions concerning principles, the first principle of armed combat or rather of command and control is the singleness of command. This refers to what the commander has to be, and the Chief of Staff -- there has to be, one body, one head, one soul, in order to ensure that everything functions properly. In this case, as many questions obviously have been raised, many issues are being raised, that did not function. Well, this is where the problem lies. I, as a soldier, would not have allowed myself to provide random assessments and to draw such serious conclusions, and this is a very serious conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: At page 90 of the transcript today, Mr. Morrissey asked you about the billeting of soldiers, specifically in relation to 200 soldiers from Sarajevo, and suggested that the corps commander would not normally concern himself with such details. My question to you arising from that is: In what circumstances could a commander of seniority such as a Corps level involve himself in details such as the billeting of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he would involve himself in such matters very rarely. The corps commander would do this very rarely. His task was to designate the sectors or zones of responsibility for certain units, and to say that such and such a battalion or such and such a brigade will be assigned such and such a sector or zone of responsibility, and that it is for the commander to decide how to deploy the unit in that sector or rather in that zone of responsibility. And this goes right down the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said very rarely. In what circumstances, what rare circumstances, could you envisage a commander - the seniority of a corps commander - involving himself in that level of detail?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours I object to this now. This is now becoming a speculative exercise, frankly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I withdraw the word "envision," then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm really asking the whole question be withdrawn as speculative, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, it can't be speculative because the witness has said "very rarely." Now, if he says "very rarely" -- he didn't say "never." He said "very rarely."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Even with that I wonder how relevant it is to our case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Highly relevant, because the Prosecution allegation is that Mr. Halilovic involved himself in the details of billeting soldiers in Grabovica, as did Mr. Karic, very senior officers. And with civilians, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may try.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What are those rare circumstances?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, let's say that the corps commander, in accordance with the norm of the command of the Supreme Command Staff is assigned a unit, a police unit, a civilian police unit, and for certain reasons that only the commander of the Supreme Command Staff is aware of, he may issue a written or verbal order to the corps commander. He may say take charge of this unit that will be deployed in your zone of responsibility and take responsibility for its accomodation, for billeting them, and then he might mention certain reasons. And then the corps commander might have to become more involved and become more involved in billeting such a unit. That is one possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. My learned colleague, Mr. Morrissey, also asked you about the SVB investigation in relation to Grabovica and Trebevic and suggested there was a reason -- Trebevic could have been a reason -- sorry, there could have been a reason to delay it until Trebevic. And your response was, "there was no reason to delay it." My follow-up question or clarificatory question is, there is no reason to delay it past when?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. That's not what I said. If you have a look at the transcript, you'll see that for yourself. I said that there was no reason in the sense of postponing the processing of Grabovica. I never mentioned Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's clarified the question I had, thank you.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were speaking about the security service, and then the Defence counsel asked me whether Arnautovic did anything or not, and whether there were any reasons to halt the Prosecution of crimes committed in Grabovica. I said that from a military point of view, there was no reason to put an end to that and Trebevic was also discussed but Trebevic is something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You -- you also in cross-examination, in response to questions from Mr. Morrissey, said that the 1st Corps I think had 70.000 troops and 40.000 were within Sarajevo. How many troops were there on the other side, encircling Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the enemy's forces?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yeah, the VRS, the Serb forces which were encircling Sarajevo in 1993. Mr. Morrissey asked you questions about the threat to Sarajevo, the number of troops you had. Specifically the Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You just want to know about the number of troops or are you interested in all the equipment that they had? I really have to be careful when I mention numbers because I can't guarantee that they are quite correct. I can only provide you with approximate numbers. I think the Sarajevo Romanija Corps that had laid siege to Sarajevo had about, as far as I know, according to my sources, which may be correct but not necessarily so, I think it had between 25.000 or perhaps 30.000 troops. It would sooner be 30.000. It had all sorts of weapons. This is very important because you will now compare the number of mren my corps had and the number of men that the Sarajevo Romanija Corps had, but you aren't bearing in mind weapons and ammunition. Men are of no importance. Men are only cannon fodder if you don't have ammunition, and if you don't have any weapons, if you don't have tanks, if you don't have howitzers, et cetera, so they were far stronger, especially in terms of technical equipment, and such supremacy has never been observed before in any other wars, anywhere in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Morrissey also asked you about I think the composition of the brigades, the ethnic composition. In case it wasn't clear, you referred to a mixed brigade. What was the percentage ethnicity of this majority of the soldiers in the 9th Motorised Brigade? Are you able to say how many -- percentage of Serbs, Croats and Bosniaks in that particular brigade? And the 10th, if you can answer that, answer both.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you about the corps. I don't know what the case was for lower units because I don't have the exact numbers. In the corps as a whole at the time, there were 70.000 or 75.000 men, 5 to 7 per cent were Serbs and 3 to 4 per cent were Croats, in the entire corps. However, it's also true to say that there were units in which there were very few men who were not Bosniaks when compared to units which were far more multi-ethnic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge El Mahdi?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Witness, there are two matters I would like to clarify, and I'd like to deal with these matters in five minutes, at the most. Firstly, I'd like to ask you about two orders that were submitted to you. You received an order dated the 2nd of September from Mr. Halilovic, and there was another order dated the 23rd of September. In the first one, reference was made to certain units and soldiers requested brigades, though the 9th and 10th Brigade and the 2nd Independent one. And in the order dated the 23rd, the reference was only made to the formation of a unit of 300-odd soldiers, and it was up to you to select them. So how do you reconcile this? Which order was more in accordance with the military needs?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a soldier, and this is something I have already mentioned in the course of my testimony, believe, and I'm convinced that it is the right of the most senior officer to draft and issue an order. In both cases, it is his legal right. And both the order issued on the 2nd of September and the one issued on the 23rd, the superior has the right to do this. But if we are discussing purely military matters, the second part of your question concerned the rule that was generally followed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting you, but which one was more in accordance with military regulations? Your corps commander or superior commander, any superior commander?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a soldier, I have to say that usually the second order would be more in accordance with military regulations, the order dated the 23rd of September 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps this is why you asked for Mr. Delic's opinion before you carried out the order of the 2nd.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That really wasn't the reason. I received an order from my superior and regardless of whether units had been named or not, all that was important for me was whether I would carry out that order, or perhaps there were some objections that the key man in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in your opinion, Mr. Halilovic did not have the authority to issue orders to you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He did have the authority to issue orders to me. He did have such authority. I could have chosen not to consult Rasim Delic. However, when constantly justifying myself and, as I have said in my subconscious, I wanted it avoid the necessity of sending units. But not for any other reasons, just because of the danger that that would have posed for the city of Sarajevo. This is what I explained to Rasim Delic. I told him that I had problems. I couldn't sends the units there. I was afraid that Sarajevo would fall. But he said, "Act in accordance with the order from the Chief of Staff," and that was the end of the matter. I complied with that order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So Mr. Delic was informed of the details?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What else could I say except "absolutely"? That's precisely how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second matter I would like to clarify concerns you. You were defending the town. In military terms, in your opinion, were there any other possibilities? Could one have used other brigades that were also defending the town, brigades other than two brigades? I'm referring to the 9th and the 10th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite frank, perhaps there was another possibility there, but not a very realistic one. Perhaps there was a possibility to use somebody from the 1st Mountain Brigade or the 2nd Mountain Brigade. Yes that might have been possible, but as for the other brigades and you have to remember that Sefer Halilovic was in Sarajevo from the first day of the war, and he was very familiar with the situation in Sarajevo, just as I was. He knew very well which brigade was deployed where, and what their responsibility was for the defence of Sarajevo. Therefore, I believe that it did not occur to him at all to ask that I send units from the 1st Vitez Brigade because Sefer Halilovic knew very well what the elevation 850 Zuc was, and what it meant for the Defence of Sarajevo. Also what the elevation Stupa [phoen] meant nor the Defence of Sarajevo. And how important the defence of Dobrinja was, where the 5th Motorised Brigade was deployed, because this is where the tunnel was where which was used by many citizens of Sarajevo, and which was a life line for the city. Now, let me tell you something about Mojbilo [phoen]. I'm now referring to all these geographical areas and this might be too much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to make sure I have understood your answer correctly, did you think that there was the possibility of using other brigades and use other elements to carry out another operation outside of Sarajevo? Would your answer be yes or no? Could you answer the question -- or could this have been done without affecting the military need of protecting the town?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may say so, this is a very good question, whether we could have used, perhaps, units from the 3rd Corps or from the 2nd Corps. Knowing the entire situation in the battlefields of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I'm speaking about the 1st Corps and the brigades that is were defending Sarajevo because you have shown us where the various brigades were deployed.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You will be very satisfied with my answer. When Sefer Halilovic sent the first order on the 2nd of September, had he perhaps not named the units at all, Delta, the 9th and the 10th Brigade, and the 2nd Independent Battalion, had he only said and had he only written the order in the same way as the order of the 23rd September was written, then I, if I were deciding on that, would have sent at least 50 per cent of the same units that I did send.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting you but I'll quote roughly the order of the 2nd. [In English] "Part of the 9th and the 10th and Solakovic, totaling 300, to be sent to Bradina where the 6th Corps command will take them over." [Interpretation] So the units were specified. However, perhaps you've confused the order of the 23rd of September. Perhaps you confused that with the order of the 23rd of September but you were given the possibility of selecting the 300-odd soldiers that were needed. So my question is as follows. I will repeat it. As someone involved in the strategy and the defence of the town, was it possible for you to select soldiers from other brigades without affecting what was needed in military terms, without affecting the military situation?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partially, probably yes. However, not to the full extent. Not in the sense of the full number of people that were needed. What I was trying to say is the following: If Sefer Halilovic had not named the units in the first order, even then I would have still sent the 2nd Independent Battalion and the Delta Brigade. He didn't even have to list them. I can guarantee you that I would have decided to send them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And why not the 9th and 10th?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will tell you why. I would have sent these units because they were reserve units, they were mobile units, they did not have an area of responsibility. Now, the question is whether I would have sent the 9th and the 10th, and I have to view this realistically. Perhaps if I did not send these two units, perhaps I would have still decided to use one of these brigades and would have used some troops from another unit. This is my reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, any questions out of the Judge's questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, well, I think during the proceedings, the Prosecution tendered a lot of documents, and the Defence made some objections. I believe that I'm in a position to make a ruling concerning the admission of those documents. The documents 378, 379, 391, 385, 392, 393, 389, 395, are admitted into the evidence. The document 380, 386, 387, P205, are not admitted into the evidence through this witness, without prejudicing the future tendering. As for the document 390, that is the intercept document, we will deal with it at a later stage. On the part of Defence, do you think you still have any documents which were not tendered?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: We don't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, witness, thank you very much indeed for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. We keep you here for more than a week. I apologise to you, but I can say to you that you may go back home and if in the future we need your assistance, I believe you'll be willing to come to our help. Thank you very much. And I would like to thank all the interpreters and the guards and the other people working for this case, since we have been sitting here for five sessions today. It is very tiring. Also taking into consideration we have a very extraordinary sun-shining day today. We will resume on the 11th of May and we'll continue our proceedings in this case. Witness, after we adjourn, Madam usher will show you out of this courtroom. We wish you a very, very pleasant journey back home. Thank you. The hearing for today is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
